real: have / don't have
note: Korean has no verb 'to have' for possession in everyday speech. 'I have time' is 시간이 있어요 — 'time exists (for me).' The owner is just understood.

real: it's delicious
note: 맛 (taste) + 있다 (exists). Its opposite, 맛없어요, is literally 'taste doesn't exist' = it tastes bad. The 'exists' pattern builds many words.

real: my mom / my house
note: Koreans say 'our' for things tied to a shared group — family, home, country, company — even when speaking only for themselves. Saying 내 엄마 ('my mom') sounds oddly possessive.

real: I'm hungry
note: The body part is the subject: 배 (stomach/belly) + 고프다. No 'I' needed — context supplies it. Same family: 배불러요 ('stomach is full') = I'm full.

real: (someone) is smart
note: Qualities are often expressed through body parts: a good head = intelligence. Its cousin 눈이 높다 ('eyes are high') means having picky standards.

real: hi, how are you?
note: A warm everyday greeting, historically rooted in times when a full meal wasn't guaranteed. Nobody is actually asking about your meal — answer 네 (yes) and greet back.

real: thanks for the meal (before eating)
note: Said before a meal to the cook or host — gratitude packaged as a promise. Its bookend, 잘 먹었습니다 ('I ate well'), is said after finishing.

real: good work today / thanks for your effort
note: The standard sign-off with coworkers, staff, or anyone who did work — acknowledging effort itself rather than results. English has no everyday equivalent.

real: you can do it! / good luck!
note: Borrowed from English 'fighting' but repurposed as pure encouragement — before exams, interviews, games. Nothing combative about it.

real: this hits the spot (even about hot soup!)
note: Famously said while eating scalding-hot soup or sitting in a hot bath. It describes the refreshed, unblocked feeling — not the temperature.

real: hey! (casual greeting in passing)
note: Between neighbors and acquaintances this is often just a greeting, not an interrogation. A vague answer like 그냥요 ('just...') is completely fine.

real: the art of reading a room
note: The skill of sensing others' moods and the unspoken situation. You can have fast 눈치, lack it (눈치 없다), or 'see 눈치' (눈치를 보다) — anxiously gauging others' reactions.

real: deep attachment that grows over time
note: The bond that accumulates between people who share time — friends, family, even a grumpy neighbor. You can have 정 for someone you don't especially like. It explains a lot of Korean social life.

real: frustrated-suffocated feeling
note: The specific feeling of a blocked chest: slow wifi, a friend who won't take advice, a stuck situation, an airless room. Physical and emotional at once — English needs a whole sentence for it.

real: bittersweet 'I wish it weren't over/so'
note: The soft regret when something good ends too soon or almost worked out — leaving a great trip, losing narrowly, a friend moving away. Not sad exactly; wistful.

real: no reason / just because
note: The universal answer to 'why?' when there is no why. 왜 왔어요? (Why'd you come?) — 그냥. It deflects gently without being rude. Massively common in real speech.

real: I like music too
note: 도 doesn't stack on the particles you know — it replaces them. 음악을도 is wrong; the single 도 carries both the 'object' job and the 'also' job at once.

real: headed there vs. doing something there
note: 에 points at a destination (or where something exists); 에서 marks where an action happens. 학교에 가요 — go TO school. 학교에서 공부해요 — study AT school. Mixing them is the classic learner tell.

real: with a friend — or 'and'
note: One particle, two English jobs. Between nouns it's 'and': 우유하고 빵 (milk and bread). After a noun, before the action, it's 'with': 친구하고 봤어요 (watched it with a friend). Context decides.

real: how have you been?
note: The standard greeting after time apart — the past tense of 지내다 (to spend time / get along). Answer by bouncing it back: 네, 잘 지냈어요.

real: I don't (choice) vs. I can't (ability)
note: English 'don't' blurs what Korean splits: 안 is a decision, 못 is inability or circumstance. 술 안 마셔요 — I choose not to drink. 술 못 마셔요 — I can't (health, driving, tolerance). Koreans hear the difference instantly.

real: I want vs. he/she seems to want
note: Korean grammar marks WHOSE desire it is. -고 싶어요 is for your own (or your listener's) wants; describing a third person's takes -고 싶어해요 — you can only report the wanting they display, not feel it for them.

real: a fried-chicken-and-beer night
note: 치킨 + 맥주 squashed into one word — a whole social institution: after-work gatherings, summer river picnics, watching the game. Korean loves these portmanteaus; learn the parts and you can often decode the whole.

real: which word depends on YOUR gender
note: Korean has four words where English has two: a woman's older sister is 언니, a man's is 누나; a woman's older brother is 오빠, a man's is 형. And they stretch past blood — close older friends earn the same titles. Age ordering is social infrastructure.

real: let's drop the formalities
note: The ritual invitation to switch from polite speech into 반말 — you 'put down' the formal language like a heavy bag. Until someone says this (or you're clearly the elder), stay in -요.

real: the same word, worn formal or plain
note: Honorifics swap whole NOUNS, not just verb endings: an elder's age is 연세, their meal is 진지, their house is 댁. You'll ask a friend's 나이 but a grandmother's 연세 — same question, different wardrobe.

real: 10:10 — two number systems on one clock face
note: Korean runs both number systems at once and the clock splits them down the middle: hours are native (열 시), minutes are Sino (십 분). Nobody knows a tidy reason; everybody does it anyway. Say a full time and you've used both systems in four syllables.

real: plans / an appointment
note: 약속 있어요 sounds like you've sworn an oath; it means you have dinner plans. The word covers everything from pinky promises to calendar entries — commitments big and small share one word, which says something about how seriously plans are taken.

real: the old count-from-one system (now mostly retired)
note: Traditionally you were born at one 살 and everyone aged together on New Year's — so 'Korean age' ran one or two years ahead of international age. A 2023 law standardized the international count (만 나이), but the old system lingers in conversation, so you'll still hear both.

real: near me / near YOU / far from us both
note: English splits space two ways; Korean splits it three: 여기 is by the speaker, 거기 is by the listener, 저기 is away from both. That's why 거기 is also 'there (where you are)' on the phone — and why pointing across the room is always 저기.

lit: go to school / go toward school
real: the endpoint vs. the heading
note: 에 pins the destination — you end up at school. (으)로 gives the bearing — you head that way, no promise you stop there. Taxi Korean runs on (으)로: 왼쪽으로, 오른쪽으로, 역으로 (station-ward).

real: cell phone
note: English parts, Korean invention — no English speaker says 'hand phone.' Konglish is its own vocabulary layer: 아파트 (apartment building), 서비스 (a freebie on the house), 파이팅 (you can do it!). Knowing English helps — and misleads.

real: I'm fine / it's okay / no thanks
note: One word, three jobs: comfort someone (it's okay!), answer 'how are you' (I'm fine), and — the one that trips learners — politely DECLINE. Offered a bag at the checkout, 괜찮아요 means 'no thanks.' Watch the hand-wave that comes with it.

real: blue — and nature's green too
note: The older word 푸르다 covered sky, sea, AND forests, and that range still echoes: a green traffic light is 파란불 ('blue light') and lush mountains are 푸른 산. 초록색 is unambiguously green — but don't be surprised when Korean calls the go-light blue.

real: the 있다/없다 adjective factory
note: Korean mass-produces adjectives by declaring existence: taste exists (delicious), fun exists (interesting), problem doesn't exist (no problem), 멋있다 — style exists (cool). Learn 있다/없다 once and whole families of words assemble themselves.

real: I'll be busy — or she's probably busy
note: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 does two jobs: about yourself it's a plan (갈 거예요 — I'm going to go); about others or the world it's an educated guess (지금 바쁠 거예요 — she's probably busy). Same ending, plan or prediction — who the subject is decides.

real: four-plus words wearing one syllable
note: 이 is the number two, a tooth, 'this' (coming soon), the subject particle, and a common surname (Lee). Hanja once told them apart in writing; in speech, context has always done the work. Korean's short syllables moonlight shamelessly — meet each 이 as its own word.

real: Korea's speed-of-life ethos
note: Doubling for urgency — 빨리 (fast) said twice is a whole national tempo: same-day delivery, sprint-speed service, elevators with worn-out door-close buttons. Koreans joke about it and take quiet pride in it. You'll hear it before you learn it formally.

real: a statement about an elder — or a request to you
note: The same -(으)세요 ending honors the subject (선생님이 가세요 — the teacher is going) AND makes polite requests (가세요 — please go). Context and intonation decide. It's why 안녕히 가세요 — goodbye — is literally 'please go peacefully.'

real: could I get some water? (softened)
note: 좀 is 조금 (a little) worn smooth — but in requests it isn't about quantity. It's a cushion, like English 'just' or 'could you…': 물 좀 주세요 asks nicely, not sparingly. Sprinkle it into any 주세요 and sound instantly more native.

real: a freebie, on the house
note: 서비스예요! from a shop owner means a free extra just landed on your table — bonus 반찬, an extra skewer, dessert you didn't order. English 'service' got imported and promoted into generosity. Respond with delighted 감사합니다.

real: I can go
note: Korean builds 'can' out of existence: 수 is a way/means, so ability = 'the way exists' and inability = 'the way doesn't exist' (갈 수 없어요). The same 있다/없다 factory that built 맛있다 and 재미있다 — existence is Korean's favorite raw material.

real: no / not allowed / no way!
note: 되다 means become-work-be-okay, so its negation is the universal veto: rules (여기서 사진 안 돼요 — no photos here), refusals, and pure disbelief. Screamed without the 요 — 안 돼!!! — it's the sound of every K-drama's worst moment.

real: the modesty deflection
note: Compliment a Korean speaker's English and you'll hear 잘 못 해요 — regardless of fluency. Deflecting praise is good manners, not low self-esteem. When YOUR Korean gets complimented (it will — 한국어 잘하시네요!), the culturally perfect return is 아니에요, 잘 못 해요.

real: it's raining
note: English needs a dummy 'it' to rain; Korean lets the weather act for itself: 비가 와요, 눈이 와요 — rain and snow are travelers that arrive. Wind gets its own verb (바람이 불어요), and rain even stops itself (비가 그쳐요). The sky is full of subjects.

real: one syllable for sky and face
note: 눈이 와요 — snow is coming. 눈이 예뻐요 — your eyes are pretty (probably). Older Korean held them apart by vowel length (snow was the long one); modern speech leans entirely on context. 눈사람 (snow-person) and 눈물 (eye-water: tears) each inherit a different 눈.

real: the summer monsoon — a season inside a season
note: For a few weeks around July, rain becomes the default state and umbrellas become clothing. 장마 has start dates, forecasts, and its own mood. Alongside 미세먼지 season and 벚꽃 season, it's proof Korea runs on many more than four seasons.

real: traffic is bad
note: No word for 'traffic jam' needed — the road itself gets stopped up, like a pipe. The same verb clogs noses (코가 막혀요) and speechless moments (말이 막혀요). One metaphor, many blockages.

real: how you address any driver
note: Korean rarely uses names with strangers — jobs + 님 do the work: 기사님 (driver), 사장님 (owner), 선생님 (teacher, or any respectable stranger). Address people by their role worn with honor, and doors open. Literally, sometimes.

real: the night's true deadline
note: Seoul's subway sleeps around midnight, so 막차 시간 quietly governs every evening's social physics — the glance at the phone, the 먼저 가요, the sprint through the station. Miss it and the night gets a taxi-fare surcharge.

real: housewarming party
note: Move into a new place and you owe your people a 집들이. Guests traditionally bring 휴지 (toilet paper) or 세제 (detergent) — long rolls and rising bubbles mean a long life and growing fortune. The host cooks; the guests admire the view; everyone asks about the rent.

real: Korean underfloor heating
note: Traditionally, kitchen smoke was routed under stone floors; today hot-water pipes do the job in every apartment. It's why floors are for sitting and sleeping, why an 이불 on the 바닥 beats a cold bed, and why shoes stop at the 현관 — you don't wear the street across a surface you sleep on.

real: I'm exhausted / so done with today
note: Said at desks, in classrooms, in queues — and, famously, while already at home. When there's no energy left for anything, the stated destination is 집, even if you're sitting in it. M3's -고 싶어요 doing emotional heavy-lifting.

real: the flattened-by-overwork illness
note: Not quite flu, not quite fatigue: the full-body collapse Korean recognizes as its own named disease — 몸살이 났어요, and everyone nods. Doctors prescribe 푹 쉬세요; grandmothers prescribe soup. That the language needs this word says something about the work culture.

real: I'm SO hungry
note: Korean hyperbole's favorite engine: [feeling] + 죽겠어요 = dying of it. 더워 죽겠어요 (dying of heat), 힘들어 죽겠어요 (dying of hardship). Nobody is dying; everybody says it hourly. English does 'starving to death' — Korean industrialized the pattern.

real: generous (always over-caters)
note: Said of the host who cooks for twelve when four are coming. The body is Korean's favorite metaphor kit: 코가 높다 (high nose — arrogant), 입이 무겁다 (heavy mouth — keeps secrets), 귀가 얇다 (thin ears — easily swayed). Glove size is not the point.

real: to take an exam
note: Korean doesn't take tests — it SEES them. 시험을 봐요 (I'm taking a test), 시험을 잘 봤어요 (it went well). English 'sits' exams in Britain and 'takes' them in America; Korean watches them happen. Same verb as seeing a movie.

real: the exam that stops the nation
note: One November morning, all of Korea holds its breath: flights are grounded during the listening section, offices open late to clear the roads, police escort late students with sirens on, and juniors cheer at the school gates. Twelve years of 학원 evenings aim at this single day.

real: you can do it! / good luck!
note: Konglish that outgrew its source: borrowed 'fighting,' repurposed as pure encouragement. Said before exams, interviews, matches, Mondays. English speakers find it adorably aggressive; Koreans find English's lack of an equivalent genuinely inconvenient.

real: social radar — reading the room
note: The skill of sensing what everyone needs without being told: when to refill a glass, when the 부장님's 'anyone busy tonight?' isn't a question, when to leave. 눈치가 빠르다 — quick radar — is high praise; 눈치가 없다 is a diagnosis. Perhaps Korean's most famous untranslatable.

real: good work today (the leaving ritual)
note: Said at every departure from shared work — leaving the office, ending a call, finishing a class. It doesn't evaluate the work; it honors the effort. English 'good job' judges; 수고하셨습니다 acknowledges. Learn it before your first Korean workplace; hear it forever after.

real: the week with no weekend
note: Take M5's weekday names, delete the weekend, photocopy Friday over it: the seven-day workweek as dark comedy. Office workers say it the way soldiers sing marching songs. Its existence — like 몸살's — is a cultural x-ray.

real: Korea's rented-room leisure economy
note: M8's humble 방 runs a business empire: rooms you rent by the hour to sing, game, or sweat. Small apartments plus dense cities equals leisure that happens in rented rooms — the -방 suffix maps an entire way of socializing.

real: hopeless at singing / dancing / directions
note: The -치 suffix names cheerful incompetence: tone-deaf, dance-clumsy, direction-blind (M14's 몸 and M12's 길 doing the describing). Declaring 저 음치예요 before the 노래방 mic is self-defense, tradition, and usually a lie told by the best singer in the room.

real: awesome! / no way! / jackpot
note: From folktale gourds that split open full of treasure. Now the all-purpose amazement word — a goal, a plot twist, a friend's news, a good 치킨 place. Positive or scandalized depending entirely on the eyebrows.

real: hello / how are you
note: A greeting, not a lunch offer — from eras when the answer wasn't guaranteed to be yes. 밥 먹었어요? is its casual twin. Answer 네 and move on; nobody is feeding anybody. Caring about someone's meals IS caring about them — the whole culture in one question.

real: eating alone (as a named act)
note: 혼자 + 밥, compressed. That Korean NEEDED this word says everything: meals were so default-communal that solo dining required naming. The family grows — 혼술 (drinking alone), 혼영 (movies alone) — as the culture makes peace with company-of-one.

real: excuse me! (to a restaurant auntie)
note: In casual restaurants, the middle-aged server is summoned as family — 이모, mom's-side aunt, the warmest title available. It buys better 반찬 refills than 저기요 ever will. Use only where aprons and floor seating suggest it; the 부장님's French place, not so much.

real: same-age peer
note: The word you've had since Module 1 has a catch: a 친구 is properly someone your OWN age. One year older and they're your 형/누나/언니/오빠, not your 친구 — which is why Koreans ask your age within minutes of meeting. Not rudeness: they're calibrating the entire relationship, 반말 included. 동갑? Instant friendship eligibility.

real: the bond that accumulates between people
note: Untranslatable heavyweight: the connective tissue that builds through shared meals, favors, arguments, time. You don't fall into 정 — it seeps (정이 들다). It survives dislike: 미운 정, the bond you have with someone who annoys you, is still 정. Friendship is 우정, family-feeling is 정 — Korea's social physics runs on it.

real: to be in the flirty maybe-stage
note: From English 'something' — as in, there's SOMETHING between them. The named stage before 사귀다: texting too often, denying it to friends. 썸 타는 중이야 — I'm riding a something. English needed this word and never made it; Korean borrowed the raw material and built it.

real: Korea's messaging operating system
note: Not an app — infrastructure. Work, family, 회식 planning, wedding invites, paying friends back: all 카톡. 카톡해! replaced 전화해! for a generation, and 단톡방 — the group chat — is where Korean social life actually lives. The yellow icon is on every phone in the country; opting out is a lifestyle statement.

real: left on read
note: 읽다 (read) + 씹다 (to chew — slang for ignoring): they READ your message and said nothing. The 1 next to your 카톡 message disappears when read — so 읽씹 is provable, timestamped, and litigated between friends accordingly. English got 'left on read' years later; Korea had already compressed it to two syllables.

real: the proof photo
note: 인증 (verification) + 샷 (shot): the photo that PROVES it — you ran, you voted, you found the 맛집, you actually met. Korean internet culture treats experiences as claims requiring evidence; the 인증샷 is the receipt. It's why the 셀카 arm extends before the food gets touched.

real: clothes make the person
note: The proverb behind every makeover scene: dress someone well and they fly. Where English clothes 'make the man,' Korean gives them wings — same wisdom, better aerodynamics. Quoted whenever someone shows up unexpectedly well-dressed.

real: luxury brands (and the culture around them)
note: 명 (name — 별명's 명) + 품 (goods): goods with a NAME. Korea is a per-capita luxury heavyweight — department-store lines before opening, first-job bag rituals. The word carries the whole phenomenon: aspiration, gifting etiquette, and the gravitational pull of a logo.

real: deliberately matching couple outfits
note: M19's 커플 + look: dressing identically ON PURPOSE — matching tees, jackets, down to 커플 신발. Peak commitment display at theme parks and Jeju. Western couples match by accident and apologize; Korean couples match by appointment and photograph it (인증샷, naturally).

real: Seoul's shared living room
note: Not just geography — infrastructure for joy: picnic blankets, rental tents, 라면 vending machines that cook it for you, and delivery 치킨 that finds your GPS pin on the grass. 한강 가자! proposes an entire genre of evening. The phrase 한강 뷰 (river view) also moves real estate prices by fortunes.

real: the seasonal pilgrimage
note: 구경 (leisurely looking) turns nature into an event: in spring the nation migrates to cherry blossoms, in autumn to the turning 단풍 — traffic jams, matching outfits, 인증샷 mandatory. The forecasts are broadcast like weather: bloom fronts move north, foliage fronts move south, and Korea moves with them.

real: someone who thinks their small world is the whole world
note: The classic proverb — the frog believes the circle of sky above its well is all the sky there is. Deployed for provincialism of every kind, including one's own: 저는 우물 안 개구리였어요 is a humble way to say travel changed you. M6's position noun 안 doing literary work.

real: food first, everything else second
note: The proverb ranks Korea's most legendary mountain BELOW lunch: even the finest scenery is best 식후 — after eating (M13's 후!) — 경 (the viewing of 경치). Quoted before every itinerary is rearranged around a 맛집. The national priorities, notarized in proverb form.

real: there's no place like home
note: 고생 (suffering) begins at your own 현관, says the proverb — beds too hard, food too strange, 짐 too heavy. Said half-jokingly while packing and wholly sincerely while unpacking. Where Dorothy needed ruby slippers, Korean needed one conditional — M20's -면, doing folk wisdom.

real: the country, shrunk to three hours
note: Seoul to Busan in under three hours — the bullet train made the whole peninsula a day trip, and 당일치기 (same-day round trip) a lifestyle. Book a window seat on the right side heading south; the 바다 appears just before 부산 and the whole carriage looks up.

real: no way! / that's nonsense
note: Fully decodable with owned parts: M4's 말 + M2's 도 + M10's 안 돼요 (here in M19's 반말). A claim so wrong it can't even assemble into speech. The reflex reaction to 소문, 거짓말, and prices in 명동. Polite version: 말도 안 돼요.

real: (very often) it's just different
note: Koreans habitually say 틀리다 (to be wrong — M15) where 다르다 (to be different — M24) belongs: 우리는 성격이 틀려요 means 'our personalities are DIFFERENT,' not wrong. Textbooks scold; speech ignores. Remember the split the other way: 맞고/틀리고 is for answers, 같고/다르고 is for comparisons — and enjoy owning a distinction natives blur.

lit: as much as you know, it is seen
real: you see what you know
note: The saying behind every museum trip (popularized by art historian 유홍준) — built on M24's own machinery: 아는 is 알다 wearing the -는 badge, ㄹ dropped. 만큼 ('as much as') is Ring 2 glue, previewed. Why the 궁 you visited in M23 gets better with every module you finish.

real: birthday ritual — or exam failure
note: Two jobs, one bowl. New mothers eat 미역국 to recover, so every birthday you eat it in tribute to yours. But said after an exam — 미역국 먹었어요 — it means you FAILED: seaweed is slippery, and you slipped right off the pass list. 시험 때 (this module's glue) it is banned from the table; that's how seriously the superstition is taken.

real: the baby picks its future
note: The centerpiece of the 돌잔치 (M22's 돌 + M25's 잔치 — the note that promised a party delivers). Objects are spread before the one-year-old: 실 (thread) for long life, 돈 for wealth, 연필 for scholarship — modern tables add microphones, stethoscopes, and computer mice. The baby grabs one; destiny is declared; the room cheers; the photo lasts forever.

real: the milestone worth a party
note: M9's 백 + M25's 일, self-assembled. Babies get a 백일 celebration — from the era when surviving a hundred days was the hard part — and couples count 백일 anniversaries before switching to years (M19's 커플 culture, timestamped). Korea counts what it treasures, in days.

real: well begun is half done
note: M8's 시작하다's noun + M5's 반 (half) + the plain copula: starting IS half the work. Quoted at every January gym, every first Korean lesson — and at the end of Ring 1, where the math finally flatters you: you started at 안녕하세요, so the rest was the other half.

real: good job / well done
note: Korean praises the STRUGGLE, not the result — 'you suffered' is the warm thing said after exams, work, and long days, kin to M16's 수고하셨습니다. The 고생 of M23's 집 떠나면 고생이다, now aimed at you kindly. Reply: 아니에요 — or say it back.

lit: to drink the kimchi soup first
real: counting your chickens
note: The full proverb: someone promises you 떡, and you drink the digestive kimchi-water before the rice cake even arrives. M6's 부터 (starting-from) doing idiom work: celebrating FROM the soup onward, prematurely. Said, smiling, to anyone planning the victory party early.

real: any middle-aged stranger
note: Korea extends the family tree to the entire country: strangers are uncles and aunts, shop ladies are 이모 (M18), older friends are 언니/오빠/형/누나 (M4). The catch: 아줌마 to a woman's face can land as 'you look old' — 이모님 or 사장님 flatters, 저기요 stays safe. The fictive-kinship system is warm, and it is a minefield.

real: (someone) is tall
note: Korean has no verb for 'to be tall' — height is a possession that is big or small: 키가 커요/작아요. Same chassis as 인기가 많아요 (M17) and 정이 많아요 (M26): pick a noun, measure it, let the subject own it. Asking someone's height: 키가 어떻게 되세요? — the polite how-does-it-become.

real: the four directions (in Korean order)
note: English says north-south-east-west; Korean says 동서남북 — east first, where the sun rises. The order is fixed like a spell: compass apps, feng-shui talk, and the idiom 동서남북을 모르다 (to not know east from west — to be utterly lost) all run east-first. M27's compass words, in their native sort order.

real: I can't sleep
note: You don't fail to sleep in Korean — sleep fails to ARRIVE. Same forecast grammar as 비가 와요 (M11) and 화가 나요 (M19): inner states are weather, and you're just the reporter. Related bulletins: 생각이 안 나요 (the thought won't surface), 이해가 안 돼요 (understanding won't engage).

lit: I shall go to school and come back
real: bye — leaving for school!
note: The departure formula every Korean child fires at the front door — M28's round-trip verb wearing M18's -겠- (the 잘 먹겠습니다 machinery). The promise built into the verb is the point: not just going — returning. The parental reply: 다녀와 (M19's 반말, warm edition), or 잘 다녀오세요 going up the ladder.

lit: even put in the eye, it wouldn't hurt
real: utterly precious (usually a grandchild)
note: The maximum-affection idiom: M28's 넣다 putting a beloved somewhere famously intolerant of foreign objects (M14's 눈 + 아프다), and the eye not minding. Grandmothers deploy it about grandchildren; couples about each other in early episodes. Anatomically alarming, emotionally exact.

real: pain, sympathy, exhaustion, or delight — context decides
note: The national sigh has four jobs: pain (아이고 허리야 — my back), sympathy (아이고, 어떡해 — oh no, you poor thing), exhaustion (the sound of sitting down after fifty — involuntary, guaranteed), and delight (아이고 예뻐라, at babies). Korean grandparents conduct entire conversations in it. Often clipped to 아이고이고이고 under real duress.

real: whatever's fine (the non-answer)
note: M29's 아무 + 거 + -나: the answer to 뭐 먹을까? that decides nothing — and, famously, the answer that means the asker must now read minds (M16's 눈치, activated). Couples cite it in arguments; menus fear it. The positive twin of 아무도 없어요's emptiness.

real: I know, right?
note: The 그렇다 machine's agreement setting: warm, low-effort, endlessly repeatable. 날씨가 덥네요 — 그러게요. Someone states the obvious; you co-sign it; society functions. Casual form 그러게, often doubled (그러게 말이야 — you're TELLING me).

real: clear lemon-lime soda — and a satisfying moment
note: The false friend of the beverage aisle: 사이다 is Sprite-style soda, no apples involved. Its slang career is better: a 사이다 moment is one that fizzes away frustration — the sharp comeback, the villain's comeuppance. The opposite is 고구마 (sweet potato): dense, dry, stuck in your throat. Korean reviews grade dramas in soda and root vegetables.

real: goosebumps — especially at couples' PDA
note: M30's 닭 + 살 (flesh): goosebumps, from cold, from horror — and, most productively, from public displays of affection. A 닭살 커플 (M19's 커플) is one whose sweetness raises bumps on bystanders. 닭살 돋아! — I've got goosebumps! — is the standard heckle, deployed with love.

real: something you can see but never have
note: M15's 그림 + M18's 떡: the painted rice cake feeds nobody. Deployed at real-estate listings, sports cars, and 딸기 뷔페 reservations that sold out. English pies live in the sky; Korean rice cakes hang in frames — both stay uneaten.

real: an iced-americano loyalist
note: 얼어 죽어도 아이스 아메리카노 — 'even if I freeze to death: iced americano' — first-syllabled into a personality type. Korea drinks 아아 through blizzards; the word salutes the commitment. M14's 죽다-hyperbole and Reading 4's shrinker, in one glass.

real: tragicomic — funny and sad at once
note: 웃기다 (M19) welded to 슬프다 (M7): the word for memes that hit too close, comedies about your own life, and 월요일 아침. English needs a sentence; Korean fused two adjectives and moved on. Conjugates like 슬프다: 웃퍼요.

real: slang about slang (meta-준말)
note: 별걸 다 줄인다 — 'they abbreviate EVERYTHING' — which is itself an abbreviation: the complaint about first-syllabling, first-syllabled. Deployed by the previous generation at the current one, forever. Reading 4's pressure rule, aware of itself.

lit: join when joining, leave when leaving
real: read the room — know when you're wanted
note: 낄 때 끼고 빠질 때 빠져라, first-syllabled: the social skill of knowing which conversations include you. M16's 눈치 as an imperative — what the 꼰대 lacks and the 인싸 has calibrated to the millimeter.

real: the strong and the weak (in any relationship)
note: Contract language escaped the contract: 갑 is the stronger party, 을 the weaker — landlord/tenant, brand/franchisee, boss/intern. 갑질 is 갑 abusing the slope; 을의 눈물 (the eul's tears) headlines labor news. Two legal placeholders that became a national vocabulary of power — and yes, that's M30's formal 과 holding them together.

lit: push / pull (in a dead politeness level)
real: every door in Korea, speaking a ghost register
note: 하오체 — the semi-formal register of period dramas — died out of speech a century ago but was never fired from signage: 미시오, 당기시오, -지 마시오, 멈추시오. Korea's doors address you like a Joseon official addressing a peer. Answer them in the same register and you've walked into a costume drama; just read, push, and pull.

real: open / currently in operation
note: The ○○ 중 machine: hang 중 (middle, 中) after any noun and it means in-the-middle-of-it — 영업 중 (open), 공사 중 (under construction), 통화 중 (on a call), 회의 중 (in a meeting), 사용 중 (occupied), 다이어트 중 (don't offer cake). One borrowed syllable runs every busy-sign, door hanger, and status message in the country.

lit: horses to Jeju, people to Seoul
real: talent belongs where it can thrive — so everyone heads for the capital
note: The full proverb: 말은 나면 제주도로 보내고, 사람은 나면 서울로 보내라 — send a foal to Jeju (the horse pastures), send a child to Seoul (the opportunity). Radar inside: this 말 is HORSE, not speech (말씀's humble cousin) — one syllable, two creatures. Centuries old and still the country's operating logic; see 서울 공화국 for what it did to the map.

real: everything in Korea concentrates in the capital region
note: Half the population lives in 서울 + 경기도 + 인천; the jobs, universities, hospitals, and broadcasters crowd in with them. 공화국 = republic (공화 + your country-국) — the phrase Koreans reach for when complaining that the other eight 도 might as well be scenery. The horse proverb is how it started; the KTX (M23) is how it accelerated.

real: all of Korea — everywhere in the country
note: Joseon carved the country into eight 도 in 1413 — 경기, 강원, 충청, 전라, 경상, plus three now north of the border (평안, 함경, 황해). The count stuck as an idiom for 'the whole country' centuries after the map moved on: 팔도 사투리 (dialects from everywhere), 전국 팔도, and the 팔도 instant-noodle brand in every convenience store. M14's 팔 + this module's 도 — two syllables, six hundred years of map.

real: sorry, what did you say? (or, with heat: WHAT?!)
note: The quote-machine as a reflex: 뭐라고 (해요) with the reporting verb dropped entirely. Flat intonation = 'come again?'; rising heat = the last thing said was outrageous. Among friends it's 뭐라고? — and in texts it shrinks further to 머라고/뭐라구. One quoting particle, the whole spectrum from hard-of-hearing to how-dare-you.

real: I hear they're coming — hearsay in one syllable
note: -다고 해요 compressed to -대요 (and -라고 해요 to -래요) — the 준말 reading's frequency-pressure law applied to grammar itself. 온다고 해요 → 온대요; 학생이라고 해요 → 학생이래요. This is gossip's native gear: 결혼한대요! (I hear they're getting married!). Recognize it now; Ring 2 will have you producing it soon enough.

real: a star the whole country has adopted
note: 국민 as a prefix nationalizes affection: 국민 여동생 (여자 + M4's 동생 — the beloved young star everyone claims as family), 국민 MC (the host in every living room), 국민 간식 (the national snack — 떡볶이 holds the title). When fifty million people agree on something, Korean files it under the family register — 우리나라 logic (M27), one shelf over.

real: please take care of me — the first-meeting formula
note: Said when joining a team, meeting in-laws, starting lessons — anywhere a relationship begins. English has no slot for it: you're formally handing yourself over and trusting the other side to be kind. Built from owned parts: M10's 잘 + this module's 부탁 + M9's humble 드리다 in M4's 합니다체. Answer it with a smile and the same phrase back.

lit: ah is one thing, eo is another
real: HOW you say it changes everything
note: A 속담 about speech itself, built from two Module-1 vowels: swap ㅏ for ㅓ and the word changes — 맛 becomes 멋 (taste becomes style, M3/M21), 살 becomes 설. So mind your delivery: the same message lands warm or cold depending on the syllable you pick. The proverb your confusables drill has been acting out since day one. Deploy it when someone says the right thing the wrong way.

real: polite formulas nobody means literally
note: 언제 밥 한번 먹어요! (let's grab a meal sometime!) usually isn't an invitation — it's a warm goodbye. 놀러 오세요! doesn't always mean come over. 빈말 (비다 empty + 말 speech) is the lubricant register: kindness performed, not promised. The test: a real invitation comes with a date (M25's machine). Don't be hurt when the meal never happens — and learn to make the noises back.

real: frazzled — too swamped to think straight
note: The national state of being: mornings, Mondays, moving day, parenthood — all 정신이 없어요. It doubles as an apology-adjacent greeting (요즘 정신이 없어서 연락 못 했어요 = sorry, life ate me) and the adverb 정신없이 means 'in a blur': 정신없이 바빴어요. The 있다-factory's spookiest product — Korean measures sanity in stock levels.

real: the Monday blues, diagnosed
note: 월요일 (M5's Moon-day) + 병 (M14's illness): the Monday blues, but Korean files it as a medical condition — and everyone claims the diagnosis. 월요병 때문에 우울해요 is a complete, socially valid excuse. The -병 suffix productively diagnoses anything: 공주병 (princess sickness — vanity), 게으름병 (chronic laziness). The five-day workweek's most honest word.

real: don't even THINK about it
note: Fully decodable ambition-crushing: M8's 꿈 + M2's 도 (even) + dream-verb 꾸다 + M19's bare -지 마. Korean dreams are 'dreamed' with their own verb (꿈을 꾸다 — cognate object, like singing a song: 노래를 부르다), so forbidding the dream forbids the wanting. Deploy on friends eyeing your last piece of 치킨.

lit: a three-year-old's habit goes until eighty
real: old habits die hard — so raise them well from the start
note: Nearly every word is yours: M5's 세 살, this module's 버릇, M30's 여든, M6's 까지, and 가다 in the plain form the quote-machine taught you to read. Korea's most-quoted parenting proverb — deployed on nail-biters, phone-checkers, and anyone whose 버릇 outlived its excuse. The pedagogy checks out: this module is literally about what sticks.

real: to fall in love — same accident, same grammar
note: Korean and English independently agreed: love is a hole you fall into (빠지다 — the same verb as falling into water). No one 사랑에 걸어 들어가다 (walks in); the grammar insists it's an accident. The verb's other jobs sharpen the joke — 드라마에 빠지다, 게임에 빠지다: obsession is just love with worse posture.

lit: a dragon rises from a ditch
real: greatness can come from humble beginnings
note: 용 = dragon, 개천 = a roadside stream: the classic rags-to-riches proverb, powered by M28's 나다 (the eruption verb — dragons ERUPT from ditches; the grammar knew). Modern Korea argues about whether it's still true — 'the ditch-dragon era is over' is a whole newspaper genre (M32 gave you the vocabulary for that debate). Either way: when a night-shift kid passes the bar exam, this is the headline.

real: what a relief — I can stop worrying now
note: Korean worry is a carried object: you hold your 마음 (M19) tight until the news is good, then 놓이다 — this module's passive — sets it down for you. Said after the call comes, the test results post, the kid texts back. The active version exists too: 마음을 놓다 = let yourself relax. English exhales; Korean puts the heart down. Same relief, better physics.

lit: I got hit by the wind
real: I got stood up
note: You dressed up, you waited, they never came — you stood in the wind and the wind is all that showed. M11's 바람 + 맞다 (to be hit — the homograph of M15's 맞다 'correct': one syllable, right answers and rainstorms). The doer's side exists too: 바람맞히다 = to stand someone up. Related but worse: 바람(을) 피우다 = to cheat — in Korean, wind is never good news for couples.

real: the silver lining — it could have been so much worse
note: The phrase Korea reaches for after every fender-bender: 불행 (불- the un- prefix + 행복's happy-행 = misfortune) + S2's 중 (amid) + this module's 다행. 다리를 다쳤지만 불행 중 다행이에요 — broke a leg, but it wasn't the neck. The 불- prefix is a machine of its own (불가능 impossible, 불편 uncomfortable — M12's 편하다 negated); file it, Ring 2 keeps paying it.

real: to let go of expectations — want nothing, hurt less
note: Korea's standing prescription for disappointment: before exam results, after breakups, during job hunts — 마음을 비웠어요 means you've released the wanting. Temple-stay Buddhism runs through it (the monks mean it literally), but so does test-day pragmatism: expect nothing, and the result can only surprise you upward. M19's 마음 + this module's 비우다: the heart as a container you can, with practice, pour out.

real: HELP! — the emergency scream
note: Not 도와주세요 (that's for directions and heavy boxes) — real danger screams 사람 살려!: make-the-person-LIVE, this module's 살리다 in the imperative, particles abandoned because emergencies don't gate. Also deployed in mock horror: buried under work, tickled by friends, facing a spider. The causative party's loudest member; may you only ever use it for the spider.

real: high-maintenance — it takes a lot of care
note: Fully decodable: M8's 손 + M17's 많이 + 가다 — your hands GO to the thing, repeatedly. Said of fiddly recipes (잡채 is the canonical example), needy pets, delicate plants, and — fondly — certain people: 손이 많이 가는 스타일. The caretaking module's own summary: everything in it, from 아기 to 화분, is something 손이 많이 가는. Affection, measured in trips.

real: overnight — all at once, out of nowhere
note: M8's 하루 + M2's 아침 + 에: change compressed into a single morning — 하루아침에 유명해졌어요 (famous overnight — M35's machine at full speed), 하루아침에 바뀌지 않아요 (it won't change overnight — every coach's caveat). Korean picked morning, English picked night; both agree real change usually takes longer than either.

lit: no gap to open eyes and nose
real: utterly swamped — not a second to breathe
note: M14's 눈 and 코 + this module's 뜨다 + 새 — and that 새 is the worn-down 사이 (gap, M6) you just met inside 요새 and 어느새: too busy to open your eyes, let alone the nose (how one opens a nose is not addressed; that's how busy). 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빴어요 = the week, summarized. The 있다-factory's most breathless product.

real: the old custom of running fashionably late
note: Konglish, self-deprecating: mid-century Korea joked that appointments ran on 코리안 타임 — 30 minutes behind, no apology needed. The 빨리빨리 era (M8's gap deck) killed it dead: today's Korea is punctual to the minute, and KTX doors forgive nothing. The phrase survives as a tease for late friends — 또 코리안 타임이야? Deploy gently; receive it never (M33's 미리 연락 exists for a reason).

real: it can't be helped — that's just how it is
note: The great Korean concession: 어쩔 (어찌 + 할 — the 'however-done' stem from M33's 어쨌든 family) + M10's way-exists machine, negated. Rain on moving day, sold-out tickets, the boss's schedule — 어쩔 수 없어요 accepts them all with a shrug that took centuries to perfect. Deploy it and locals will assume you've lived here years; it's the sound of Korean equanimity.

real: hard work always pays off
note: Study-culture scripture, written on desk stickers and gym walls: this module's 노력 + 배신하다 (to betray — a drama-vocabulary loan worth keeping) + M28's -지 않다 in the plain form the quote-machine taught you to read. Athletes tattoo it, 수험생s (M15's world) whisper it, and skeptics note that 재능 (talent) never signed the contract. Believe it anyway; it's load-bearing.

lit: picking a star from the sky
real: next to impossible
note: M11's sky and star, plus 따다 (to pick/pluck — apples, licenses, and here, stars): the impossibility idiom — 서울에서 집 사기는 하늘의 별 따기예요 (buying a Seoul apartment = star-picking; M31's 서울 공화국 gap agrees). Note the -기 nominalizer (M13) turning the whole heist into a noun. When 불가능하다 feels too clinical, reach up.

lit: to grip sweat in one's hand
real: nail-biting — edge-of-your-seat suspense
note: Three of this module's words in one clench: the palm sweats (땀), the hand closes on it (쥐다), and the tension holds. Usually worn as a badge: 손에 땀을 쥐는 경기 (M17's 경기 — a match watched with wet fists), 손에 땀을 쥐는 영화 (M2's 영화). English bites its nails; Korean grips its own weather.

lit: to laugh so your belly button falls out
real: to laugh yourself silly
note: M35's 빠지다 — the faller-outer of teeth and weight — applied to the navel, with -게 turning catastrophe into a degree: laughed TO THE POINT OF navel loss. 배꼽 빠지게 웃었어요 = we were in stitches. Anatomy objects; comedy insists; M7's 웃다 does the work either way.

real: the deadline is HERE — panic mode, now
note: M36's great faller delivers M13's 불 onto this module's 발등: when fire lands on the top of your foot, you stop planning and start hopping. 발등에 불이 떨어졌어요 = it's due tomorrow and I've done nothing. M38's 미루다 is how the fire got scheduled; M15's exam culture keeps the matches.

real: the bond that grows through friction as much as fondness
note: M26's untranslatable 정 meets this module's 밉다: long relationships accumulate BOTH kinds — the affection from good times (고운 정 — 곱다, lovely, ㅂ-family like 밉다 itself) and the stranger attachment that grows through quarrels, annoyance, and years of putting up with each other (미운 정). Old couples cite it, siblings embody it, and 정떨어지다 — jeong falling off — is the only real divorce. You can 미워하다 someone and be bound to them anyway; Korean saw no contradiction and named it.

lit: to want to hide in a mouse hole
real: to be dying of embarrassment
note: 창피함's official escape plan: 쥐 (mouse) + 구멍 (hole) + M37's 숨다 + M3's -고 싶다 — when the embarrassment peaks, Korean shrinks you to mouse size and starts scanning the baseboards. 너무 창피해서 쥐구멍에 숨고 싶었어요 = I wanted to disappear. The proverb cousin promises the mouse hole its day in the sun (쥐구멍에도 볕 들 날 있다 — even mouse holes get sunshine); until yours arrives, it remains an emergency exit.

ko: 기쁨은 나누면 배가 되고 슬픔은 나누면 반이 된다
rom: gippeumeun nanumyeon baega doego seulpeumeun nanumyeon bani doenda
lit: joy, divided, becomes double; sorrow, divided, becomes half
real: share your feelings — it multiplies the good and shrinks the bad
note: The proverb runs entirely on this module's -ㅁ factory: 기쁨 and 슬픔, freshly minted, plus 나누다 (to divide/share — worth keeping) and M35's 되다 doing the arithmetic. Radar inside: this 배 is 倍 (times, double) — not M3's belly — and 반 is M5's half, keeping its old job. Korean emotional culture in one equation: feelings are meant to be split among people, and the math always favors telling someone.

real: the flavor that comes from the cook's own hands
note: M8's 손 + M18's 맛: the conviction that the same recipe tastes different depending on WHOSE hands made it. 할머니 손맛 is the gold standard; restaurants advertise 어머니의 손맛 like a certification. It's why 김장 (M26) uses no measuring cups — just hands that know how much 고춧가루 is enough. Science shrugs; Korea does not argue with grandmothers.

real: you'll get nothing — no mercy, no leftovers, no second chances
note: In a broth-first food culture, 국물 is the minimum a meal owes you — so denying even THAT is total denial: 늦게 오면 국물도 없어요 = show up late and you get nothing. M2's 도 (even) plus M1's 없다 do the threatening; the kitchen supplies the metaphor. Another negative-polarity build, straight from M39's school: Korean measures scarcity in soup.

real: to rain on the parade — deflate the mood, spoil the plan
note: 식초's 초, weaponized: dump vinegar into a dish and the flavor collapses, so 초 치지 마세요 = don't ruin this for me (said mid-plan, mid-dream, mid-toast — with M14's -지 마세요 doing the pleading). M17's 치다 handles the splash. English brings rain, Korean brings vinegar; both agree somebody always arrives with the wrong liquid.

lit: gather dust and it becomes a great mountain
real: small savings add up — every little bit counts
note: The savings culture's founding document: 티끌 (a dust mote — worth keeping) + M17's 모으다 (gathered: 모아, the ㅡ dropping as taught) + 태산 (the legendary great mountain — China's Mt. Tai, proverbially the biggest thing imaginable). It's 조금씩 저축하세요 as folklore, printed inside bank apps and said while dropping 동전 into jars. Works beyond money too — study minutes, gym visits, vocabulary words: this app is a 티끌 모아 태산 operation and admits it.

lit: the salary grazes the bankbook and goes
real: the pay is gone the moment it lands — rent, bills, and card payments take it all
note: The modern office worker's lament, alive in every group chat around 월급날: M16's 월급 arrives in this module's 통장, and 스치다 (to graze, brush past — the verb K-dramas use for near-touch moments, worth keeping) is all the contact they get before autopay sweeps it out. The plain-form -ㄴ다 ending is the one M32's quote machine taught you to read. Same physics as this module's 받자마자 다 써요 sentence — except here nobody even got to do the spending.

lit: the throat is the police bureau
real: one must eat — hunger will drive a person to do anything, including work they hate
note: M14's 목 (throat) + 구멍 (hole — the one M42's embarrassed mouse hid in) + 포도청, the Joseon dynasty's thief-catching bureau: the throat COMPELS the way the law does, so people take the 야근, keep the awful 직장, sell what they'd rather not. Said with a sigh while accepting unpleasant work: 목구멍이 포도청이라… — 'well, the throat is the police bureau.' Grim, ancient, and still filed under: reasons everyone showed up Monday.

lit: in studying, there is no royal road
real: there are no shortcuts in learning
note: Euclid told a king there was no royal road to geometry; Korean filed the ruling under 공부. M26's 왕 + 도 (the way-道 inside 태권도, M26) + M1's 없다: even kings walk the whole path. Desk-sticker canon beside M39's 노력은 배신하지 않는다 — study culture quotes itself in proverbs, and this one closes every shortcut you were about to search for.

ko: 서당 개 삼 년이면 풍월을 읊는다
rom: seodang gae sam nyeonimyeon pungworeul eumneunda
lit: after three years, even the schoolhouse dog recites poetry
real: hang around long enough and it rubs off on you
note: 서당 is the old village school — hanja by rote, one stern teacher; 풍월 is wind-and-moon poetry; the dog is unqualified and succeeds anyway. 삼 년 (M2's 삼, M25's 년) of proximity beats zero years of talent — said to comfort anyone learning by osmosis. If you've been marinating in dramas and song lyrics: you are the dog, and it's working.

real: the sticky exam-day gift
note: Before big exams Koreans gift 엿 (taffy) and 찹쌀떡 (sticky rice cake — M18's 떡, at its stickiest), and M35's 붙다 taught you the physics: passing IS sticking (시험에 붙다), so you eat sticky things to adhere to the list. The inverse superstition already sits in M25's gap deck — slippery 미역국, banned from the exam-week table. A complete folk science of admission, run entirely on texture.

real: beauty is in the eye of the beholder — attraction is a personal prescription
note: M14's 눈 wearing M21's 안경: a lens ground for exactly one person — which is why your friend's baffling boyfriend makes perfect sense to her. Said with a shrug whenever 매력 refuses to be argued: 제 눈에 안경. The proverb concedes what this module's vocabulary keeps measuring — 매력 is real, but the instrument is never calibrated the same way twice.

lit: the outside is one way and the inside is another
real: two-faced — the public self and the private self don't match
note: M41's 겉 (the surface) and M28's 속 (the interior), audited by M24's 다르다 twice over and linked with M10's -고. The four-word integrity test this module was built to fail or pass: when someone's 이미지 and 성질 never meet, this is the filing. The compliment is its negation — 겉과 속이 같은 사람, someone whose outside and inside agree.

ko: 열 길 물속은 알아도 한 길 사람 속은 모른다
rom: yeol gil mulsogeun arado han gil saram sogeun moreunda
lit: you can know ten fathoms of water, but not one fathom of a person's insides
real: you never really know anyone — people are deeper than water
note: M5's 열 and a 길 that isn't the road: M12's radar gains a tenant — 길 the fathom, an old body-length unit for depth. M39's -아/어도 concedes the easy half (water, transparent to ten lengths) before the verdict: a person is opaque at one. M28's 속 holds both meanings down. Filed beside 눈치 (M42) as the reason the radar has to exist at all.

real: stop making things up — quit spinning theories
note: 소설's job description, weaponized: when someone's speculation outruns the facts — who likes whom, why the boss frowned — Korean tells them to stop drafting fiction. M14's don't-machine at its bluntest (-지 마), usually dropped to 반말 because the accusation is rarely formal (소설 쓰지 마세요 exists for politer conspiracies). The internet grades especially florid theories 소설 쓰네 — 'writing a whole novel over there.'

real: watch it live at airtime — fandom's ratings duty
note: 본방 (the first-run 방송 — not the rerun, not the stream) + 사수 (死守, defend to the death — a military word, chosen on purpose). Ratings still crown winners in Korean TV, so fandoms mobilize to watch live and be counted: 본방 사수하세요! closes every cast interview. The 시청자 as soldier; appointment television as an oath — and after today you can parse both halves.

real: a bookworm — a devoted reader
note: 책 (M1) + 벌레 (M22): the same insect English keeps, but in Korean the bug is a productive SUFFIX for anyone consumed by a habit — 공부벌레 (study-grind), 일벌레 (workaholic), 잠벌레 (champion sleeper). Affection and mild concern in equal parts. The 독자 every publisher dreams of.

real: blood is thicker than water — people side with their own
note: M14's 팔 + M6's 안 + 굽다 — but NOT M18's grill-굽다: this is its homograph, bend-굽다, and the pair even split conjugations (grilling goes ㅂ-irregular, 구워요; bending stays regular, 굽어요). Anatomy as ethics: an arm physically cannot bend outward, so of course the judge favors his 조카. Said with a shrug to explain favoritism — or to excuse your own: 팔은 안으로 굽는다잖아요.

real: a parent hopelessly besotted with their daughter
note: M4's 딸 + M44's 바보: a parent — classically a father — rendered foolish by his daughter: camera roll full, wallet photos ready, objectivity zero. Not an insult but a claimed identity: 저 딸 바보예요, said proudly. The mold extends wherever love beats dignity — 아들 바보, 조카 바보, 손자 바보 — and this module stocks every target.

real: life under the husband's family — the hard lot of the traditional daughter-in-law
note: 시집 + 살이 (living, from M4's 살다): the bride's traditional existence inside the 시집, under the 시어머니's command — measured in labor, patience, and silence. A whole folk-song genre runs on it, and the proverbial verdict says the chili is hot, but 시집살이 is hotter. Modern Korea largely dismantled the arrangement; the word stays employed describing residue — and any workplace with a tyrannical boss: 회사 시집살이.

lit: ten years, and even the rivers and mountains change
real: given enough time, everything changes — the decade as Korea's unit of deep change
note: Every part already yours: 십 (M2) + 년 (M25) + M20's -(으)면 + 강 (M22) + 산 (M11) + 도 + 변하다 (M26), in the plain -ㄴ다 form M32's quote machine taught you to read. 강산 — rivers-and-mountains — is Korean for the land itself, and the proverb is why 년대-thinking runs so deep: ten years remakes the skyline, the neighborhood, and you. Said while revisiting a hometown, an old school, or a photo album.

real: time heals — grief, breakups, embarrassment: the calendar is the prescription
note: M35's 세월 note flagged this proverb in passing; here is the full filing. 세월 — time as the heavy thing that passes — plus M10's 약: Korean prescribes the calendar for what no pharmacy stocks. Said with a pat on the shoulder to the freshly heartbroken, usually as 세월이 약이야. The gap deck's gentlest entry, and the one you will eventually test yourself.

lit: I didn't know time was going
real: I completely lost track of time — the highest compliment to good company
note: Keep it frozen: 시간 (M1) + 가다 (M1) wearing the -는 badge that M24 named + 줄 (a dependent noun for facts-you-supposed — a Ring 2 machine for a later module; today it stays welded inside this phrase) + M4's 모르다, past tense. Said after good conversations, good books, and every successful date: 재미있어서 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요. It's 어느덧, reported from inside the moment.

real: one's go-to karaoke song — the number you always sing
note: 십 + 팔 (M2's numbers) + M12's counter 번: 'number 18' = your signature 노래방 song, the one your friends groan at and demand anyway. The origin is a loan: kabuki's eighteen greatest plays (jūhachiban) became Japanese slang for 'best routine,' crossed the strait, and settled into Korea's singing rooms. 제 십팔번은... is a formal self-introduction in any 노래방; the standards body suggests 애창곡 instead, and the whole country keeps saying 십팔번.

real: the national cheer — the country's name stretched over five claps
note: M31's 대한민국 note promised you a stadium chant; here is the filing. Born in the 2002 월드컵: shout the country's name with the first syllable stretched — 대~한민국 — then clap the answer: 짝짝-짝-짝-짝. Millions in red did it in every 광장 (M23) until the rhythm became national infrastructure; start the claps anywhere in Korea today and the room will finish them. A whole country as one 응원 section — the loudest thing this module teaches.

real: quit while you're ahead — exit at the top
note: 박수 + 치다 (M17) wearing M25's -(으)ㄹ 때, then M23's 떠나다 in the plain command form M32's quote machine taught you to read: leave WHILE the applause is still going, not after it dies. Said of retiring athletes, long-running shows, and third helpings at dinner. The advice every 스타 hears and almost none of them take.

lit: even going sideways, as long as you reach Seoul, it's fine
real: any road will do if it gets you there — ends over means
note: 모로 (sideways, crabwise) is the fossil — it barely exists outside this proverb; the rest is all yours: M39's -아/어도 concedes the crooked route, M30's 만 narrows the goal to one city, and 가면 된다 is M23's -(으)면 돼요 wearing the plain -ㄴ다 form M32's quote machine taught you to read. The destination is not incidental: for six hundred years, getting to 서울 (M12) has been the Korean definition of arriving — the whole 중심/지방 tension, folded into one shrug about methods.

lit: there's no gap to set a foot in
real: packed solid — rush-hour trains, festival streets, any place that went viral
note: M14's 발 is yours; the phrase carries the rest frozen: 디디다 (to set your foot down) wearing the prospective -(으)ㄹ badge you've met inside -(으)ㄹ 때 (M25), and 틈 (a crack, a sliver of space). When even one footfall can't find floor, the place is FULL — 주말의 명동은 발 디딜 틈이 없어요. The rush-hour 전철's official condition, and the highest compliment a 맛집 can receive.

lit: even the tiger comes if you talk about it
real: speak of the devil — the person you're discussing walks in
note: Korea's speak-of-the-devil keeps its apex predator on call: gossip loudly enough and even a 호랑이 materializes. Every part is yours — 도, M4's 말, M20's -(으)면, M1's 오다 in the plain -ㄴ다 form M32's quote machine taught you to read — except 제, which here is not M17's humble 'my' but its reflexive cousin: 'its OWN talk'. Deployed with a grin the second the discussed party enters the room, usually trailing off at 호랑이도 제 말 하면…

lit: to ride the heat / ride the cold
real: to suffer badly from heat / from cold — to be the sensitive one
note: M6's 타다 at its strangest job: not boarding a bus but being RIDDEN by a season — 저는 더위를 많이 타요 = summer wrecks me, the standard self-diagnosis when someone melts in June or shivers in October. The pattern is a whole susceptibility machine: 부끄럼을 타다 (blush easily), 가을을 타다 (catch autumn melancholy — the annual national mood). What you 타다, you can't help.

lit: the days when tigers smoked tobacco
real: once upon a time — the folktale opener for a very long time ago
note: Korean fairy tales don't start 'once upon a time'; they start when tigers still smoked — often at full length: 옛날 옛적 호랑이 담배 피우던 시절에, where M24's 옛날 brings 옛적 along as its archaic echo. You own the strange parts already: M14 taught both 담배 and 피우다, M46 taught 시절; the -던 is a looking-back badge from a later module — today it stays frozen in the formula. Also deployed sarcastically about anything outdated: that phone is from the tiger-smoking era.

lit: even Geumgang Mountain comes after the meal
real: food first — even the world's best sight can wait until you've eaten
note: 금강산 — the Diamond Mountain, Korea's most storied peak, across the northern border — stays frozen; the rest decodes: 食後景 is 식사's food-食 (M3), the after-後 that M5's 오후 and M13's -(으)ㄴ 후에 carried for you, and 경치's view-景 (M22). Deployed at every trailhead and palace gate the moment someone's stomach growls: itinerary second, lunch first. The national travel philosophy in seven syllables.

real: there's no place like home — travel is glamorous until you're actually in it
note: Every part is yours: M1's 집, M23's 떠나다 (the verb 'for chapters'), M20's -(으)면, and M39's 고생 — hardship, the thing Korea praises you for surviving — in the plain -이다 form laws of nature are written in. Said by parents as you pack, and by you, sincerely, three days in when the 숙소 has no hot water. The proverb 배웅s you out the door.

real: to get ripped off — pay tourist prices
note: 바가지, the hollowed-gourd scoop of old kitchens, stays frozen; the verb is M10's 쓰다 in the wear-sense its note filed under headgear. Somehow having a bowl planted on your head became paying triple, and the grammar assigns blame: the vendor 씌워요 (M37's causative — puts it ON you), you 써요. 바가지 요금 = rip-off pricing — the accusation every 관광지 review stands ready to make; check the menu before the seafood arrives.

real: noise from the apartment upstairs — Korea's #1 neighbor conflict
note: M13's 층 + 간 (the between-間 that M40's 간식 note sliced out of 시간) + 소음 (騷音, noise — untaught, riding frozen: clamor-騷 plus the sound-音 inside M26's 발음). In a country that lives stacked, footsteps overhead are national policy: there are government mediation centers, a soundproof-mat industry, and a steady drumbeat of news stories. The etiquette arsenal runs from a note in the elevator to the dreaded doorbell at ten; the sentence deck files the symptom, 잠을 못 자요.

real: a close neighbor is as good as family
note: M13's 이웃 note made this exact promise — 'neighbor-cousins: the saying that a close neighbor beats a distant relative' — and here is the full filing. The 사촌 (四寸, four-degrees-removed: a cousin — untaught, frozen here) is who the neighbor outranks: the long form runs 먼 사촌보다 가까운 이웃이 낫다, with M22's 보다 doing the ranking and M14's 낫다 the judging. Born when villages shared their 마당s; tested daily now by the gap deck's other entry.

lit: gives the illness, then gives the medicine
real: hurt someone, then play the healer — kindness after harm doesn't cancel the harm
note: Every brick is Ring 1: M14's 병, M9's 주다 twice, M10's 약, chained by M10's -고 and closed in the plain -ㄴ다 form M32's quote machine taught you to read. Said of the friend who insults your cooking and then compliments your apron, the boss who cuts the budget and buys pizza — the order of operations IS the accusation. Deploy it with a raised eyebrow, not a raised voice.

lit: medicine bitter in the mouth is good for the illness
real: harsh advice helps — the unpleasant truth is the effective one
note: M10's 쓰다 note flagged the bitter sense ('as an adjective, bitter') — here it finally works, wearing M24's badge: 쓴 약, the bitter medicine that M14's 입 refuses and M14's 병 needs. Korea deploys it to justify criticism roughly one breath before delivering the criticism — if you hear this proverb, brace. The contrast-는 on 병에는 is M8's old trick, still seasoning sentences.

ko: 몸이 천 냥이면 눈이 구백 냥
rom: momi cheon nyangimyeon nuni gubaek nyang
lit: if the body is a thousand nyang, the eyes are nine hundred
real: nothing you have matters like your eyes — protect them first
note: M9's 천 prices the whole 몸 (M14), M2's 구 and M9's 백 price the 눈 (M14's), and M20's -(으)면 sets up the ledger; the fossil is 냥 — the old brass coin that survives only in proverbs and historical dramas. The accounting says your eyes are ninety percent of you, which is why grandmothers cite it against phone screens in dark rooms — and why the 안과 waiting room believes it.

real: begin and you're already halfway — the hardest part of any job is opening it
note: Every part is yours: M8's 시작하다 lends its noun, M5's 반 does the arithmetic, and the plain -이다 form laws of nature are written in closes the equation. Korea deploys it at gym sign-ups, first classes, and the blank first page of every 논문 — including, once upon a time, your Module 1. You are living proof of the math.

lit: dust gathered makes a great mountain
real: small things add up — save the pennies and the fortune builds itself
note: 티끌 (a dust mote) and 태산 (泰山 — the great mountain of Chinese legend) both ride frozen; the working part is M17's 모으다, 'the collector's verb,' mid-collection: 모아. The national argument for the savings account, the vocabulary app, and the 500-won jar on the fridge — every rep you log in this course is one 티끌 on the pile.

lit: fix the barn after losing the ox
real: the countermeasure arrives after the disaster — too late, and everyone knows it
note: 소 (the ox) and 외양간 (its barn) ride frozen; the machinery is yours — M28's 잃다 loses, M13's 고치다 repairs, M10's -고 orders them wrongly on purpose, and the plain -ㄴ다 M32's quote machine taught you to read closes it like a verdict. This is the proverb Korean news reaches for whenever 대책을 마련하다 happens one 사고 too late — the editorial page's favorite barn.

lit: a chicken instead of the pheasant
real: the next-best thing will do — a workable plan B
note: 꿩 (the pheasant) rides frozen; the rest is yours: M39's 대신 — instead — and M30's 닭. Old New Year's soup wanted pheasant; pheasants are hard to catch; a chicken went in the pot, and the proverb has blessed every substitute since. Deployed with a shrug when the first choice is sold out, closed, or seeing someone else — the plan-B national anthem, three syllables of pure pragmatism.

lit: if the price is the same, the crimson skirt
real: same cost — take the prettier one
note: M24's 같다 wearing its badge, M20's -(으)면 setting the condition, M21's 치마 wearing the color; 값 (price) and 다홍 (deep crimson) ride frozen. If two things cost the same, why not the beautiful one? Korea's official permission slip for the nicer option — quoted over menus, phone upgrades, and 원룸 listings, anywhere the spreadsheet ties and the heart casts the deciding vote.

ko: 가는 말이 고와야 오는 말이 곱다
rom: ganeun mari gowaya oneun mari gopda
lit: only if the going words are lovely are the coming words lovely
real: speak kindly if you want to be spoken to kindly — speech round-trips
note: The grammar is all yours: M24's badge puts 가다 and 오다 to work as 가는/오는, and M39's -아/어야 sets the only-if condition its module drilled. The fossil is 곱다 (to be fine, lovely — untaught, riding frozen; a ㅂ-irregular, so 고와야). Deployed as a referee's whistle mid-argument: the tone you send is the tone you get back — 상대 included.

lit: even a sheet of blank paper is better lifted together
real: many hands make light work — even trivial jobs go better shared
note: 백지장 (白紙張, a sheet of white paper) and 맞들다 (to lift together — 들다 M28 with a facing partner) ride frozen; the rest is owned: M2's 도 concedes 'even', M20's -(으)면 sets the condition, and M14's 낫다 judges — in its comparative job, the one M38's 훨씬 note flagged with 이게 훨씬 나아요. Quoted whenever someone refuses help out of politeness; the paper does not care who carries it. 나머지는 같이 하면 돼요.

real: 'Is that kid THAT kid?' — four identical syllables, sorted entirely by pitch (Gyeongsang)
note: In 표준어: 걔가 그 애야? (M55's 걔, two shelves ago). In 경상도: the same four-syllable 가 — and a native speaker parses it instantly, because the southeast kept the PITCH ACCENT standard Korean flattened out: which 가 rises tells you which 가 is the kid, the subject particle, the question. The party-trick sentence of Korean dialectology, and proof that 사투리 is systems, not slang. Longer versions exist (가가 가가가?) and are deployed on Seoul friends as a hazing ritual.

real: the national joke about Chungcheong speech-speed — the warning arrives after the boulder
note: The setup: a 충청도 son sees a boulder (M22's 돌) rolling toward his father and calls out — but by the time the unhurried -유 lands, so has the rock. Korea's most retold dialect joke, and 충청도 tells it about itself with pride: the region's real signature isn't slowness but UNHURRIEDNESS — a courtesy of never rushing you, packaged with the ambiguity of 괜찮아유. (굴러가유 = 굴러가요, rolls-along — riding frozen.)

real: the most famous 사투리 line in Korean film: deflecting an offer back at the offerer
note: From 친구 (2001), the Busan gangster classic — one friend offers the other an escape to Hawaii and gets the escape handed back. 니 is the southern 네/너 (dodging the 내/네 sound-collision the confusables drill knows all about), 가라 is the plain command M33 taught you to read, and the word order is pure shrug. Quoted nationwide whenever anyone deflects a chore: 설거지? 니가 가라. The line made 부산 사투리 briefly the coolest sound in Korea — the export pipeline's proof of concept.

ko: 콩 심은 데 콩 나고 팥 심은 데 팥 난다
rom: kong simeun de kong nago pat simeun de pat nanda
lit: where beans were planted, beans come up; where red beans were planted, red beans come up
real: you reap what you sow — results follow what was actually planted, no exceptions
note: A promise kept twice over: M40's 콩 note already quoted the short form (콩 심은 데 콩 난다), and M40's 뿌리다 note said farmers' seeds are 'where every harvest proverb begins' — here is the full harvest. Every part but one is yours: 심다 (this module) wearing the -(으)ㄴ badge (M24), the place-데 (M55), M28's 나다 sprouting on schedule, the -고 connector (M10), and the plain -ㄴ다 close laws of nature are written in. Only 팥 (the red bean) rides frozen. Deployed about parenting, politics, and half-studied exams — the ledger of the soil never miscounts.

lit: reading scripture into an ox's ear
real: talking to a wall — careful explanation wasted on someone who won't take it in
note: 소 unfroze one shelf ago, and its first idiom job is patience: M14's 귀 receives, M2's 읽다 nominalizes through -기 (M13), and 경 (the Buddhist sutra — riding frozen) goes unheard. The ox isn't stupid in this proverb — it simply has other priorities, which is exactly how it feels to explain twice. Parents say it about children, teachers about phones-out classrooms, and IT departments about password rules.

real: even the expert slips — mastery doesn't cancel mistakes
note: 원숭이 (the monkey) rides frozen; everything else is owned — the even-도 (M2) concedes the expertise, M22's 나무 supplies the tree, M36's 떨어지다 does the falling, and the plain -ㄴ다 closes it like a law of nature, which it is. Crucially deployed as COMFORT, not mockery: said to the veteran who just fumbled, the native speaker who misspelled, the chef who burned the rice. You will want it handy for your own Korean.

lit: a college student in pattern only
real: in name only — the label without the substance
note: Take 무늬, add the only-particle 만 (M30), prefix any title: a 무늬만 대학생 (M15) never opens a book, a 무늬만 부부 (M25) share only the registry, a 무늬만 사장님 (M9) has no actual say. The pattern without the tiger — Korean files hollowness as a textile problem. Endlessly productive, and best deployed on yourself for charm: 저는 무늬만 학생이에요.

real: to draw THE line — set a boundary and mean it
note: The C-sense of 금 at work: not gold but the LINE — the mark chalk leaves and floors crack into. 긋다 (to draw a line, riding frozen) is ㅅ-irregular, seat four in the family M14's 낫다 opened and M40's 젓다 and M54's 짓다 filled: 그어요, 그은. Negotiations, relationships, and siblings sharing a room all end the same way — 금을 긋고, this side mine, that side yours.

lit: the navel is bigger than the belly
real: the extras outgrew the main thing — shipping that beats the item price
note: Every word is already yours: M3's 배 in its belly career (that note filed pear and boat too), 배꼽 (M41 — anchor of the polite bow), the comparative 보다 (M22), and M1's 크다. Deployed at checkout whenever the 배송비 (shipping fee, riding frozen) beats the item, or when the wrapping outclasses the gift. The anatomy is impossible; the economics are daily.

lit: did you go-and-come-back from the army?
real: standard small talk between Korean men — service status as biography
note: M28's round-trip verb — the same one the 학교 다녀오겠습니다 formula (M28's gap deck) sent to school — aimed at the year and a half that sorts Korean male biographies into before and after. The answer calibrates everything: which years the stories come from, who outranks whom in shared suffering, whether mud-season 축구 counts as a hobby. Foreign men get asked too; 'my country doesn't have conscription' is a legal answer and a reliable conversation-extender.

real: the rank choreography — doors, elevators, first bites, and beer pours all run in seniority order
note: 먼저 (M8) — whose own note taught the office goodbye 먼저 가요 — promoted to a traffic rule: the 선배 walks first, sits first, lifts the spoon first; the 후배 holds the door and pours with two hands. Reversed — 후배 먼저 — it becomes a graciousness the 선배 collects credit for. Watch any company dinner seat itself and you'll see this sentence running silently.

lit: having somehow done it, when I looked
real: one thing led to another — the all-purpose opener for outcomes nobody planned
note: 어쩌다 (do-somehow) + 보니 (upon seeing): glance up mid-life and find yourself somewhere. There is real grammar inside the chunk, but Koreans deploy it whole, as one word of fate — careers, marriages, and hobbies all officially begin with 어쩌다 보니, because taking credit for your own success is bad manners.

real: one problem solved, a bigger one waiting — it never ends
note: M36's 넘다 doing the climbing, M11's 산 doing the multiplying. Sighed at bureaucracy, renovations, and level bosses: you crest the ridge that was blocking the view, and the view is another ridge. Deploy it with a slow exhale for full effect.

real: the yelp — Korean's 'oh my god, you scared me', said BY the startled person
note: 깜짝 wearing the casual copula M19's 반말 chapter installed (이에요 → 이야): the jump itself, blurted as a complete sentence. Said with a hand on the chest, usually followed by scolding whoever caused it — 깜짝 놀랐잖아! (M42's -잖아요, stripped to 반말: you KNOW you startled me). English screams a word; Korean names the flinch. Often warmed up with 아이고 in front, which doubles the drama for free.

real: together but independent — the Korean philosophy of shared life with breathing room
note: Three adverbs, all yours: today's 따로, M29's 또, M9's 같이 — and together they name a whole social contract: couples with separate hobbies, friends who order 따로 and eat 같이, grown children living apart who gather every 명절. Restaurants run the doubled form at the register (따로따로 계산해 주세요 — M9's 계산하다, split evenly); families run this one at the scale of a lifetime. The rare idiom that is pure grammar: no frozen words, just three adverbs holding hands at arm's length.

ko: 잘되면 제 탓, 못되면 조상 탓
rom: jaldoemyeon je tat, motdoemyeon josang tat
lit: if it goes well, my doing; if it goes badly, the ancestors' fault
real: claiming credit for success while outsourcing blame — the human default, named
note: This module's 잘되다 and its unlisted cousin 못되다 (go badly — riding frozen) run the fork through the -(으)면 condition (M20), while M17's 제 claims the good half. Two fossils ride frozen and glossed: 탓 (blame — the accusatory cousin of this module's 잘못) and 조상 (ancestors — a later shelf's word). Quoted with a raised eyebrow whenever a teammate inherits the blame; the proverb's real target is always the speaker.

real: the national kind-speech campaign — the poster phrase for talking properly
note: Two of this module's adjectives wearing M24's badge on M4's 말: 바르다 supplies the correctness, 곱다 the kindness. The phrase hangs in every elementary classroom and broadcast-standards office in Korea — the institutional answer to playground trash talk, and the reason M57's proverb about words that round-trip (가는 말이 고와야…) rings like a school bell to Korean ears.

lit: it's much-fortune that it stopped at that much
real: thank goodness it wasn't worse — the accident scene's official consolation
note: 그만하다's adjective reading in its natural frame: the damage measured out at that-much and no further, and M36's 다행 — whose note filed it 'said after every near-miss' — banks the relief. The -기 nominalizer (M13) plus a clipped 을/를 gives 그만하길. Said over fender-benders, sprained ankles, and burnt dinners: Korean gratitude runs on comparisons to worse.

real: the application didn't go through — the frozen refusal every Korean office prints on your clipboard
note: The application chain (신청 → 등록 → 제출) at its dead end: 등록 — this module's second link, the putting-on-the-books — refuses the 되다 slot, and M3's 안 wedges itself in to say no. It's not that you didn't file; the machine looked at the file and closed. The single most useful phrase in any government office, where a polite '안 돼요' is all the explanation you'll get for why the queue still moves without your name in it.

real: I have no standing to apply — the polite refusal that ends the conversation before it starts
note: The application axis judged at its front door: your qualification (자격 — the paper that says you are allowed in) is absent (M1's 없다), and the thing it gates is the application (신청). The whole office chain — file, register, submit, confirm — collapses into one closed door the moment the office checks the single document you don't have. You've learned every step past it; this is the step that decides whether the past exists for you.

real: diplomacy's fundamentals — the first-principles frame for dealing with the outside
note: The outside-meeting (외교 — the crossing of borders into a meeting) wearing M57's 기본 (the basics): the phrase a briefing reaches for when the argument is about first principles, not tactics. 외교 is the noun this module hands you raw (nations meeting across a line); the frozen phrase is what it becomes in a policy memo — not the deal on the table, but the rules the table stands on, the same rules a firm runs with 자격 and 제한.

real: the woman of the house — the matriarch who runs the home, a term of warmth and deference
note: The inner room (anbang, this module's heaviest room) doing a job it can never quite do alone: naming the person at its head. 마님 is the native title of the woman who owns a house — the elder, the matriarch, the one whose name carries the whole home. In the old hanok this is the woman who sits in the anbang; in the modern apartment it's the mother-in-law you address with a small bow. One syllable of deference you don't need to be a woman to use — it's a way of honoring the person who runs the house, whoever that is.

real: a city that does not sleep — the late-night lights, the all-night bustle, the city's waking
note: Three hanja stacked into a word: 불 (M13's 불, the flame) + 야 (night) + 성 (city). The city where the fire doesn't go out and the night doesn't take over — the all-night city you see from a high window at 2 a.m., the bars still lit, the delivery drivers still on the road. A three-syllable picture of a city that decided to stay awake: the same city as the anbang's quiet, just on the other side of the wall, on the other side of the sleep.

real: to press forward with; to force through; to push someone or something onward
note: Combines S2's 밀다 (push) with M37's 붙이다 (attach). The push that carries the object the rest of the way — a nudge turned into a shove, a half-measure turned into a full one. S2's 밀다 is one push; 밀어붙이다 is the push that does not stop until the thing is moved. The push family's forceful end.

real: to fall into the water; to sink into the water
note: Binds M1's 물 (water) with M35's 빠지다 (fall in, sink in). M1's 물 is the same word the module's spill and pour verbs run out through; here it is the water that goes the wrong way, down, into the thing. Run-out is out through a lip; fall-in is down into the water.

real: don't even THINK about it — permission denied at the fantasy stage
note: This module's 꾸다 negated one stage before action: not only may you not DO it, you may not run the preview in 꿈속 (M65). The 도 (M2) delivers the 'even'; -지 마세요 (M14) does the forbidding, stripped here to bare 반말 마. Parents, bosses, and rom-com rivals all issue it; the genre-mandated response is to keep dreaming.

real: secondhand embarrassment — they did the cringe, I carry the shame
note: Internet-era Korean for vicarious embarrassment: someone else does the embarrassing thing and the 부끄러움 lands on YOU — a friend's karaoke solo, a parent haggling loudly. 몫 (share, portion — untaught, riding frozen) is the slice that falls to a person; this module's 부끄러움 turns out to be transferable property, exactly the kind of THING the -(으)ㅁ freezer promised feelings could become.

real: to click as a team — coordination so smooth it needs no words
note: This module's 손발 judged by M15's 맞다 — the fit-right verb of 맞아요: when two people's hands and feet land in rhythm, the work disappears. Said of kitchen partners, doubles teams, and comedy duos — 우리는 손발이 잘 맞아요. Its dark mirror, 손발이 안 맞다 (M3's 안), explains most group projects.

real: well-connected — knows someone everywhere
note: M14's 발 measured with M13's 넓다, whose note taught the ㄼ-batchim dance (널따 before consonants, 넓어요 with vowels). Wide feet cover ground, and covered ground means faces known: 그 사람은 발이 넓어요 = they know EVERYONE. The metaphor is walking-era sociology — your network was wherever your feet had been.

real: to not bat an eye — unshakable composure
note: M14's 눈 counted out by M5's 하나 and refused by M3's 안: not even ONE blink. The mimetic 깜짝 (the startle-flinch — riding free and glossed) is the same syllable that jumps in a surprise party's 깜짝 파티. Said admiringly of poker faces, nervously of villains — this module taught you what the body says; this idiom is the body saying nothing, on purpose.
