real: 'thanks to you' — the all-purpose gracious reply, said whether or not the other person did anything
note: 잘 지냈어요? asks after you; 네, 덕분에요 answers by handing the asker the credit — this module's 덕분 doing its politest work. They didn't water your plants or pass your exam; Korean courtesy credits them anyway. The long form, 덕분에 잘 지냈어요 (M23's 지내다), is the set reply every textbook drills because every Korean actually says it.

real: Buddha's birthday — the late-spring lantern holiday, a national day off
note: The holiday's official name is a whole grammar lesson: this module's 부처 + the -님 of M16's ladder, then 오다 (M1) lifted by the honorific -시- and wearing M24's badge, landing on M11's 날 — 'the day he honorably came.' For weeks before it, 연등 (lotus lanterns — riding frozen) hang in rivers of color over temple courtyards and shopping streets; the 절 (M26) throws its gates open, and everyone comes for the lanterns whether or not they come for the Buddha.

lit: if it gets far from the eye, it gets far from the heart too
real: out of sight, out of mind — distance in the eyes becomes distance in the heart
note: This module's 멀어지다 twice — once from M14's 눈, once from M19's 마음 — hinged by -(으)면 (M20) with M2's 도 supplying the 'too'. The bare -ㄴ다 ending is the proverb register M35's 이루어지다 note already showed you in 꿈은 이루어진다: dictionary-form present, no 요. Koreans quote it about long-distance couples and friends who moved abroad — the conveyor running on hearts, twice in one breath.

real: to be overwhelmed by sleepiness — drowsiness arriving all at once, like a downpour
note: This module's 쏟아지다 with M28's 잠 as the liquid: sleep doesn't come, it POURS — the same verb as 비가 쏟아지다, aimed at eyelids. 수업 시간에 잠이 쏟아져요 (M10's 수업, M1's 시간) is the honest student's confession, and 잠을 자다 (the doubled pair M28's 잠 note taught) is what it leads to. Korean files drowsiness under weather; the umbrella is coffee.

lit: nothing is visible to the eye
real: blind with rage — so worked up that nothing and no one in front of you registers
note: This module's 뵈다 in its FIRST dictionary sense — M36's 보이다 contracted — wearing the -는 badge from M24, on M14's 눈, with M17's 것 squeezed to 게 and M1's 없다 closing: nothing shows up to the eye. Said of someone charging ahead in fury (화가 나서 눈에 뵈는 게 없었어요 — M19's 화나다), and by elders AT the young and reckless: 눈에 뵈는 게 없어? = have you lost your senses? A set phrase is where the contracted verb survived; this is the one to recognize.

real: I know, right? / tell me about it — the commiserating agreement
note: This module's 글쎄 plus M4's 말 in the casual copula M19 installed (말 + 이야): the hedge that suddenly agrees completely. Someone sighs 요즘 너무 바빠 — 글쎄 말이야 = tell me about it. The polite floor says 글쎄 말이에요, the formal 글쎄 말입니다. Radar: 글쎄 alone commits to nothing; 글쎄 말이야 commits to everything the other person just said.

lit: a hundred hearings are not equal to one seeing
real: seeing is believing — go and observe it yourself
note: 百聞不如一見, a Chinese four-character line Korean speaks whole: M9's 백 (hundred) + hear-聞 (the 문 of 신문, M8), then the un-prefix 불- that M39's 불가능하다 note credited to the M36 gap deck + 여 (like) + M2's 일 (one) + the view-見 that M56's 발견하다 note lifted from 의견. The observer's proverb, and this module's thesis: the 과학자 who 관찰하다-s beats the hundred who only heard about it. Said 뱅무니 부려일견 — 백's ㄱ nasalizes before ㅁ, and 불's ㄹ slides onto 여.

real: the four-drum percussion ensemble — 꽹과리, 징, 장구, and the 북 — Korea's loudest folk music, and the reason 사물 has a homograph
note: 四物놀이: four-四 (M2's 사, wearing hanja) + thing-物 + M26's 놀이 — four instruments standing for thunder, wind, rain, and clouds, played by farmers' bands and now by every university 동아리 (M69) with a rehearsal room to lose. M51's 북 note called it the drum's heartbeat; this module's 사물 (事物, matter-thing) is a DIFFERENT 사 in the same spelling. The radar catch is the culture: when a Korean says 사물놀이, count to four.

real: that's just the thing / a perfect fit — the standalone verdict, no adjective needed
note: This module's 딱 promoted to a predicate: the adverb plus the copula (the 이에요 that M4's 선생님 first wore, in 선생님이에요) and nothing else — the click IS the review. 이 옷은 너한테 딱이야 (M7's 옷, M19's 너, the casual copula) = this is SO you; 점심으로 딱이에요 (M3's 점심) = perfect for lunch; 딱이네요! (-네요 from M26) = oh, that's just right. Where English reaches for 'perfect', Korean says the lid landed on the right box.

real: why bother? / was that really necessary? — the one-word retort
note: This module's 굳이, alone, with a rising tone: someone announces they'll drive forty minutes to return a pen, and the whole reply is 굳이? — must you? It judges your own choices too: 굳이 갔어요 = I went, though nobody needed me to. Said 구지, by the ㄷ+이 rule the word's own note filed beside M9's 같이; the flatter you say it, the more it means.

real: everyone fends for themselves — the survival idiom of the news cycle
note: 各自圖生: this module's 각자 + the plan-圖 that M64's 시도하다 decoded ('圖 (plan)') + 生, life — the 생 of 학생 (M4). Four hanja in a row, the classic 사자성어 shape (a four-character idiom — riding frozen), and it went from old proverb to headline: 각자도생 사회 (M32's 사회) = a society where nobody is coming to help. Said with a shrug about housing, jobs, and the pandemic years — the cold mirror of M62's 따로 또 같이.

lit: the other person's rice cake looks bigger
real: the grass is always greener — what others have always looks better than what you hold
note: This module's 남 owning M18's 떡 (the rice cake its note hands out for moving day, birthdays, and exams), measured by M9's 더 ('더 커요 — bigger') and judged through -아/어 보이다, the seen-as machine M36's 보이다 note unmasked ('is SEEN as cool'). The bare -ㄴ다 is the proverb register M35's 이루어지다 note showed in 꿈은 이루어진다. Its sibling has hung in the gap deck since M30: 그림의 떡, the rice cake you can see but never eat — this one you could eat, and you still want the neighbor's.

lit: if you like free things, you go bald
real: there's no such thing as a free lunch — the folk warning against loving freebies
note: This module's 공짜 + M1's 좋아하다, hinged by -(으)면 from M20 and landing on M10's 되다 in the bare -ㄴ다 proverb register: love free stuff and you'll end up 대머리 — bald head, riding frozen (a native 대, not the big-大, in front of M8's 머리). Nobody believes the hair part; everyone quotes it — at the friend who never pays, the uncle who hoards hotel soap, and yourself at the sample counter. The 공짜 grin, with a warning label.

real: to take care of some business — and, with a straight face, to use the restroom
note: This module's 볼일 with M1's 보다, the verb already welded inside it: doing what needs doing. 볼일 좀 보고 올게요 = I'll take care of something and be right back — which is exactly why the same sentence is the polite way to leave for the bathroom: 볼일(을) 보다 is the euphemism Korean uses where English says 'the restroom', and 큰 볼일 / 작은 볼일 (M1's 크다 and 작다, badged) sort number two from number one. Say it to excuse yourself; never ask which kind.

lit: to be turned over at the first eye
real: love at first sight — to fall for someone the moment you see them
note: The homograph's home: this module's 반하다 in its OTHER sense — to fall for — on M46's 첫 + M14's 눈 (the eye) + 에. Radar, and it catches everyone once: the 첫눈 here is first-glance, not the first snow of M26's 첫눈, though the syllables match to the letter and both belong to dramas — couples meet under one and fall by the other. 첫눈에 반했어요 is the confession; 반한 사람 (the badge from M24) is the one you fell for. Said 천누네 — the ㅅ shifts before ㄴ, the same slide the M26 sentence deck filed as '천누니'.

real: in contrast to this; on the other hand — the editorial's pivot
note: This module's 반하다 (反, its B-row sense) frozen into a connective: M29's 이 standing alone as a pronoun + 에 + 반해 = counter to this. It opens the second half of a comparison in print and on the news — 수출은 늘었다. 이에 반해 수입은 줄었다 — the contrast-sibling of M56's 또한 (moreover) and 한편 (meanwhile), completing the shelf S2's stiff connectives began. Speech says M7's 그런데, or 반대로 — M24's 반대 + M6's 로; the sentence deck runs it in 합니다체 (M4). Register, not grammar: recognize it everywhere, write it when you argue.

real: the priority seats at the ends of every subway car — and the etiquette that empties them
note: 老弱者席: the old-老 that M47's 노인 note decoded + 약 (weak — the 弱 inside M63's 약하다, decoded here; NOT M10's 약, which is 藥, medicine) + the person-者 that M27's 환자 note introduced + 석 (seat — riding frozen). The seats stay empty even on a packed train, and this module's 양보하다 is the verb that keeps them so: 자리를 양보하다 is expected everywhere in the car, but in the 노약자석 it is not a courtesy, it is the rule — a young person sitting there draws stares and, occasionally, a lecture. Newer cars add the pink 임산부 배려석 (for expectant mothers — riding frozen) at the middle doors. The whole system is M12's 자리 with a moral attached.

real: one's sleep schedule is flipped — up all night, asleep all day: jet lag, night shifts, exam season, and the school break
note: This module's 밤낮 as the subject of M35's 바뀌다 — it happened to you, nobody did it — the sentence Korea says about jet lag (시차 — the time difference, riding frozen), the night shift, 시험 기간 (M38's 기간), and every student's August. 밤낮이 바뀌었어요 is the confession, and the sentence deck says it with -아/어 버리다 from M52 for the regret; the cure is one brutal day of not sleeping, M38's 밤새다 run in daylight. Korean names the disorder with the two words it welded and puts the night first; English says the clock is off.

real: a one-off holiday the government declares by cabinet decision — usually to bridge a weekday between a 명절 and a weekend
note: This module's 임시 + 공휴일 (공 public + 휴일 — the pattern M25's 연휴 note glossed, rest-휴 + M25's 일): a holiday that exists exactly once, by cabinet decision, announced weeks ahead and sometimes days. The classic move is bridging — a Monday or Friday wedged between M25's 추석 and a weekend, so a 연휴 grows from three days to five or six; the announcement trends, and half the country reopens its 예약 apps (M52). Its cousin 대체 공휴일 (the substitute holiday — riding frozen) is the automatic one, granted when a holiday lands on a weekend. Read the word on the news and you know one thing for certain: someone's 일정 (M23) just changed.

real: the Korean winter's weekly rhythm — three freezing days, then four milder ones — and the folk phrase everyone still says when the cold snap breaks
note: 三寒四溫: M2's 삼 and 사 in hanja, 한 (cold-寒 — riding frozen; not the one-한 of M46's 한때) and the warm-溫 of M49's 온도 ('溫度 warm-degree'). The old observation that a Korean winter breathes in sevens — the Siberian high presses down for three days and relaxes for four — filed as a four-character idiom the way the M73 gap deck filed 각자도생. Forecasters still use it, grandparents still plan by it, and the internet updated it: 삼한사미 — three cold days, four days of M11's 미세먼지 — is the current, grimmer version. Say it when the thaw comes; everyone will nod.

real: to have no sense of rank — to treat elders and juniors alike, which Korean does not admire
note: This module's 위아래 hung on M1's 없다: the vertical axis turned social. The two ladders the M47 lesson named ('Korean runs TWO politeness ladders') are the up and the down; a person who 위아래가 없다 climbs neither — 반말 (M19) to an 어른 (M24), first through the door, first to the food. Said by elders about juniors, almost never the reverse, and it is the verdict behind every these-kids-today. The compliment form exists too: 위아래를 알다 (M4's 알다) = to know one's place — which in Korea is praise.

lit: to learn from over the shoulder
real: to pick up a skill by watching someone do it — never formally taught, often better than school
note: This module's 너머 welded onto M14's 어깨 and aimed through M6's 로 at M2's 배우다: learning from the far side of someone's shoulder. It is how apprentices learned before there were courses — and how most Koreans say they learned to cook (엄마 어깨너머로), to fix things, to pour a drink properly. The spelling is the module's law in one word: 너머 the noun, because you were standing beyond the shoulder, not crossing it. Said with modesty about your own skills and with a little awe about a 할머니's (M4).

real: tetraphobia — hospitals and older buildings skip the 4, because 사 (four) is also 死 (death)
note: This module's 숫자 with a superstition attached: M2's 사 (four) sounds exactly like the hanja for death, so the floor gets a letter — F, for four — the way Western hotels skip the thirteenth. Look for it in hospital elevators and older apartment blocks; newer towers have mostly stopped, but gift etiquette has not: never four of anything to someone in a hospital bed. The lucky 숫자 is 7 — M36's 행운 note ran 행운의 숫자 — and 3 does well too: 삼세판 (best of three, riding frozen) is how Koreans settle everything from rock-paper-scissors to the bill.

real: the new-driver sticker on the rear window — and the mercy it buys on the road
note: This module's 초보 + 운전, the noun inside M10's 운전하다 — the same bare 운전 that M75's 양보하다 note ran on highway signs as 양보 운전 — printed on a sticker and stuck to the back of every newly licensed car. No law requires it; the culture supplies it, and increasingly with jokes: 아이가 타고 있어요 (with M4's 아이 and M6's 타다 — the baby-on-board cousin), 저도 제가 무서워요 (with M24's 무섭다 — I scare myself too). What it buys: a wider gap, fewer horns, and a licence to stall at the light while the 택시 (M6) behind you sighs instead of leaning on the horn. Peeled off after a year or so — or never, by drivers who have learned what it is worth.

real: a third-year high-schooler — in Korea, a household identity rather than a grade
note: 고등학교 3학년 (M15's 고등학교, M15's 학년) clipped through this module's 고교 and read 고삼, with M2's 삼. The M15 gap deck owns the exam day — 수능, 'the exam that stops the nation'; this entry owns the person the year makes: the 고3 gets the quiet room and the late dinner, skips the 명절 (M25) trip, and hears 고3이니까 as the reason for everything — 우리 집에 고3이 있어요 is said the way other countries announce an invalid in the house, and neighbours lower their voices. 수험생 (exam-taker, riding frozen) is the formal word; 고3 is the one parents whisper. The identity ends the day the 수능 does — the freed 고3 gets a haircut, a phone, and a driving lesson, hence 초보 운전, one entry over.

ko: 언니의 남편은 형부, 누나의 남편은 매형
rom: eonniui nampyeoneun hyeongbu, nunaui nampyeoneun maehyeong
lit: an 언니's husband is 형부, a 누나's husband is 매형
real: in-law titles fork by the SPEAKER's gender, exactly as 언니/누나 did — whom you call what depends on who you are
note: The speaker-gender grid M4 started (형/오빠, 누나/언니 — who you are decides what you call your older sibling) runs into the in-laws: a woman's 언니 (M4) has a 형부 (this module); a man's 누나 (M4) has a 매형 (妹兄 — riding frozen), M27's 남편 either way. The younger side forks too: a younger sister's husband is 제부 to a woman and 매제 to a man (both riding frozen), and M58's 형님 note already showed kinship outranking gender in the other direction — a wife calling her husband's older sister 형님. Korean does not ask who the husband is; it asks who YOU are — the grid the M47 md drew ('Korean kinship is a coordinate system, not a word list'), with the speaker sitting at the origin. Learners get this wrong in one direction only: a man saying 형부 marks himself, gently, as having learned Korean from his girlfriend's dramas.

lit: even cold water has an up and a down
real: there is an order to everything, even a glass of water — the elder is served first
note: This module's 찬물 hung on M76's 위아래 with M1's 있다: the positive law whose negative g_m76_wiaraega_eopda already filed ("위아래가 없다 = to have no up-and-down — no sense of rank"). If even water — free, cold, poured from the same 병 (M5) — goes to the eldest first, then everything does: who sits where, who lifts the spoon first (the M18 md's table rule), who gets the first 술잔. Said by an elder, half smiling, to a junior who reached for the glass; said by the junior about themselves, it is an apology. The proverb is the whole 술자리 in seven syllables.

real: a turf war — departments, agencies, or professions fighting over who owns a job and its budget
note: This module's 밥그릇 + M67's 싸움 ("싸우다 (M19) + -(으)ㅁ: the fight, frozen solid enough to count"): the bowl is the livelihood, so fighting over bowls is fighting over jobs. It is the newspaper's word for two ministries claiming one policy, two unions claiming one worksite, doctors and pharmacists claiming one prescription — never a fight about rice. Its verbs run the same metaphor: 밥그릇을 지키다 (M26's 지키다) = protect your position, 밥그릇을 뺏기다 (frozen — to have it snatched) = lose your job to someone. Korean measures a career in bowls; the M1 word for rice was the word for a living all along.

ko: 두 손으로 따르고 두 손으로 받기
rom: du soneuro ttareugo du soneuro batgi
lit: pour with two hands, receive with two hands
real: the 술자리 etiquette: never pour your own, pour for elders with both hands, receive with both, and turn away to drink
note: M18's 건배 note has the clink ("Juniors clink lower and turn slightly away to drink"); this entry has the pour, which comes first. Rules, in order: you never fill your own 술잔 — someone fills it for you, and you watch theirs; the bottle goes in two hands (M5's 둘 on M8's 손, M32's 따르다 doing the pouring — its note ran 물을 따라 주세요 for water) when the receiver is older, and the glass is held in two when the pourer is; a junior turns the head and shoulders away to drink; an empty glass is an invitation and a full one is a refusal. The sentence deck runs the receiving half as a rule (받아야 돼요); the grammar is the obligation machine from M10, the culture is the politeness ladder of M4 holding a bottle. Learners get one thing wrong reliably: filling their own glass, which reads as a small announcement that nobody is looking after you.

real: the safety-first slogan painted on every construction fence and factory wall — and 안전 불감증, the named national failure to feel danger
note: This module's 안전 + M22's 제일 (that note: literally 'number one') — two bare nouns, no verb, the way the fence talks: 안전 제일 on the green mesh around every 공사 site (S2), on the hard hats, on the factory floor. Its shadow is a diagnosis: 안전 불감증 (riding frozen — 불- the emptier the M36 gap deck named, the feel-感 of M42's 감정, and the -증 of M53's 증상) = safety-insensitivity syndrome, the phrase the news prints after every preventable accident, from a ferry to a stairwell. The two are read together: the slogan is what the wall says, 불감증 is what the country says about the wall. Print's bare roots at their most serious.

real: the people hired the same year as you — the one office bond that rank cannot touch
note: 입사 (riding frozen — the enter-入 of M12's 입구 + the company-社 of M32's 사회) + this module's 동기 in its 同期 sense: the intake. M43's 사원 note filed the new hires as 신입사원, 'suits still creased'; a year later they are each other's 동기, and the bond outlasts the suits. In a 위아래 (M76) office the 동기 are the only people you never have to place: M19's 반말 both ways from the first week, M16's 회식 survived side by side, promotions compared in silence for decades. The army says it loudest — 동기 사랑 나라 사랑 (frozen: loving your intake is loving your country) is painted on barracks walls in M58's 군대 — and the university version, 대학교 동기, is the sentence deck's ten-year friendship. Rank is what the company assigns; 동기 is what the calendar assigned, and the calendar wins.

real: to black out from drinking — the night is gone from memory, as if the reel snapped mid-scene
note: This module's 필름 as the subject of M36's 끊기다 — the passive that note filed for calls and power ('modern life is a list of things that 끊기다'), aimed at memory: the film in the projector snaps, the screen goes white, and the rest of the evening never got recorded. 어제 필름이 끊겼어요 is the morning-after confession at every 회식 (M16) table, and the questions that follow it — 어떻게 집에 왔어요? — are M1's 집 and M23's 돌아오다 territory. The metaphor is analog and everyone under thirty still uses it; nobody has seen a reel snap, but the word 필름 kept the job. Korean names the blackout by the medium; English names it by the darkness.

real: chicken feed — a price so small it is not worth mentioning; 껌값이에요 = it's nothing, it's dirt cheap
note: This module's 껌 + 값 (price — the native price-word M21's 가격 note called its own formal twin; riding frozen as a standalone): the price of a stick of gum, as the unit of nothing. 껌값이에요 is how a friend waves off the cost of something they just bought you — M7's 싸다 in its idiom form, cheaper than 싸요 — and 껌값도 안 돼요 (with M10's 되다) = it doesn't even come to gum money, said of a wage, a fine, a lottery win. The word fossilized when gum cost a coin; gum now costs more, and the idiom has not noticed. Say it about money only, never about a person's work — that is 헐값 (a throwaway price, riding frozen) territory, and unkind.

real: the indoor golf simulator bar — a booth, a projector, a real club and ball, and a city block's worth of them in every downtown
note: 스크린 (screen — riding frozen; the loan for the projection surface, where M20's 화면 is the display) + this module's 골프: Korea's actual golf. The 골프장 costs an executive's afternoon and a two-hour drive; the 스크린 골프 booth is under the office, open past midnight, and priced per hour like M8's 방 note's 노래방 — the rented-room economy g17_bang filed, now with a driving range in it. Groups book it after 회식 (M16), beginners learn there before ever seeing grass, and the swing data on the wall is the same the pros use. Rule 3 in spirit: English parts, Korean assembly — a Korean company invented the industry, and the phrase has no English original.

lit: to hold out a duck's foot
real: to deny flatly, feign innocence — the interrogation-room verb, the caught-red-handed shrug
note: This module's 오리 + M14's 발 (the duck's foot — the webbed one, and the swimmer's flipper) + 내밀다 (to stick out, riding frozen). The story under it: the man caught stealing a chicken (M30's 닭) holds out a duck's foot and says that is what he was carrying — the evidence is right there, and it is the wrong animal. 오리발 내밀지 마 (-지 마세요 from M14, casual) = don't play dumb; 끝까지 오리발을 내밀었어요 — M28's 끝, M6's 까지 — = denied it to the end — the drama's police room, the toddler with jam on his face, the politician at the podium. English says stonewall; Korean names the exact wrong foot.

ko: 여우 같은 아내, 곰 같은 아내
rom: yeou gateun anae, gom gateun anae
lit: a fox-like wife, a bear-like wife
real: the two-type wife cliché — the fox charms and manages, the bear endures and never complains; a dated frame that every Korean still recognizes on sight
note: This module's 여우 and M49's 곰 ("The bear — and Korea's first mother") on M24's 같다 in its badge form (같은 — the like-machine's adjective coat), with M27's 아내 twice: the fox-wife reads her husband (M42's 눈치), praises him, gets her way; the bear-wife works, endures, and says nothing. The old joke has the punchline built in — men say they want the bear and marry the fox — and mothers-in-law once graded daughters-in-law on the axis. Told honestly: it is a cliché from an older marriage, and the words are still everywhere: 여우 같다 is a compliment with a raised eyebrow, 곰 같다 is affection with a sigh — both usable about anyone, either sex, any age. The 처럼 from M41 gives the adverb versions: 여우처럼, 곰처럼.

real: a contrary child — someone who does the opposite of whatever they are told; and the tale of why frogs cry when it rains
note: 청 (the blue-green hanja twin M49's 푸르다 note filed — riding frozen) + this module's 개구리: the small green tree-frog, and the folk tale it stars in. The young frog does the reverse of everything his mother says — sent to the 산 (M11), he goes to the 강 (M22); told to sleep, he plays. Dying, she reasons in reverse and asks to be buried by the river, hoping he will do the opposite and choose the hill; grief makes him obey for the first time, and now every rain (M11's 비) threatens her grave, so the frogs cry at the riverbank. That is why 개구리 croak when it rains — and why a 청개구리 is any kid, employee, or partner who cannot take a suggestion straight: 우리 아이는 청개구리예요. The moral is aimed at children; the sadness is aimed at parents.

lit: a needle thief becomes a cow thief
real: small wrongs, left alone, grow into big ones — the proverb parents say over a pocketed eraser
note: This module's 바늘 + M36's 도둑, whose note quoted the line first ("바늘 도둑이 소 도둑 된다 — the needle-thief becomes the cow-thief"), + M59's 소 + M10's 되다 in the bare dictionary form proverbs keep. The needle is the smallest thing a child can steal, the cow the biggest thing a farm owns, and the proverb draws the straight line between them: it is said to a child caught with someone else's pencil, quoted in the news about a first small bribe, and thrown at yourself the third time you take office pens home. The English cousin is the one about pennies and pounds, but Korean's version is about character, not thrift — the thief grows, not the sum.

real: the lap blanket on every Korean office chair — the desk-worker's private heating, from October to April
note: M14's 무릎 + this module's 담요, stacked bare the way Korean names kit: a blanket for the knees. Every office in the country has one per chair — patterned, fleece, often a gift with a bank's logo — because the building's heating is set by someone else and the 에어컨 (M11) runs cold well into autumn. It lives on the lap under the desk, moves to the shoulders in a long meeting, and is the one object the M43 workday never lists. Cafés lend them in winter; airplanes hand them out; 무릎 담요 하나 주세요 is a sentence that works in both. Wrap, not bedding — M13's 이불 stays home; the 담요 goes to work.

real: the all-night wholesale run — shop owners from every city buying next week's stock between midnight and dawn
note: M31's 동대문 + M38's 새벽 + M3's 시장, three bare nouns: the market inside this module's 동대문시장 that only opens when the retail one shuts. From around ten at night the towers around the gate switch to 도매 (wholesale — riding frozen): buyers with rolling carts and rolls of cash, shopkeepers from 부산 (M12) and 대구 (M31) who drove up after closing, motorbikes shuttling bags to the 고속버스 터미널 (M50's 터미널) for the dawn departures. No fitting rooms, no single pieces, prices in the plural — and by six in the morning the same streets are quiet. It is the supply chain of every small clothing shop in the country, run on the 새벽 hours M38 said Korea refuses to sleep through; DDP (riding frozen) next door is the building tourists photograph while the real business happens across the road.

real: on another level entirely — out of one's league, in a class of its own; said of a rival, a restaurant, a girlfriend's new boyfriend
note: This module's 급 as a bare subject of M24's 다르다: the grade differs. The ladder under it is real — TOPIK's 일 급 to 육 급, the taekwondo belts, M81's 고급 above 초급 and 중급 — and the idiom borrows its authority: 급이 달라요 concedes that the other side is not merely better but on a rung you are not on. Praise or surrender, tone decides (M29's 때문 note taught that rule for blame; it holds for rank): a fan says it of a singer, a losing team of the winner, a friend of the apartment you cannot afford. The 2010s' 클래스가 다르다 (클래스 — class, riding frozen) is the same sentence in a loanword; 급 is the older, shorter, and still the one the older generation reaches for. Never about yourself unless you are joking.

real: barking up the wrong tree — you have come to the wrong person, the wrong place, the wrong idea; 번지수를 잘못 짚었어요 = you've got the wrong end of the stick
note: This module's 번지 + 수 (number — the Sino 數 inside M76's 숫자, riding frozen as a suffix) as a bare subject of M15's 틀리다: the address on the envelope names a lot that is not this one. Born in the 번지 era, when finding a house meant matching a number to a plot, the idiom outlived the system — the road-name addresses of 2014 did not retire it — and it means every kind of misdirection: the complaint filed with the wrong office, the apology aimed at the wrong person, the argument that answers a question nobody asked. 번지수가 틀렸어요 is the polite way to say you are talking to the wrong man; 번지수를 잘못 짚다 (짚다 — to put a finger on, riding frozen) is the same wrong guess as a verb of your own doing. English aims at a tree; Korean aims at a lot.

real: the payphone booth reborn as a safety booth — a lockable glass box on the night street with an emergency button, a camera, and a defibrillator, kept because the law still requires a public phone
note: 안심 (peace of mind — the 安 of M4's 안녕 and the 心 of M19's 마음, riding frozen) + 부스 (booth — riding frozen; the loan that also names the photo booth and the trade-show stall): what became of this module's 공중전화. The phones outlived their callers — M6's 핸드폰 took the job by the early 2000s, exactly as M83's 전화기 note said it took the landline's — but a public line is a legal obligation, so the boxes stayed on the corners, and the telecom found them new work: press the button and the door locks, the camera records, a siren sounds, and the police (M16's 경찰) are dialled; a defibrillator hangs on the wall for the other kind of emergency. Some booths lend an umbrella (M9's 우산); the phone itself still works. The drama's rain-soaked confession was made from this box; its sequel is a woman walking home at two in the morning with a glass room to step into. Korea does not tear down the obsolete; it gives it a second job.

lit: if it goes badly, the ancestors' fault
real: blaming anyone upstream when a thing fails — the proverb's second half, quoted alone as an accusation of buck-passing
note: The other half of g_m63_jal_tat (잘되면 제 탓, 못되면 조상 탓), which rode both 탓 and 조상 frozen; M69's 조상 landed the ancestors ("M63's gap deck already blamed them (못되면 조상 탓, with this word riding frozen)") and this module lands the blame, so the half that gets quoted alone finally has all its words. 못되다 (go badly — still riding frozen) through -(으)면 from M20, then M69's 조상 + this module's 탓, stacked bare: the fault of the forebears. Said alone, it is the accusation — 못되면 조상 탓이지 — thrown at the colleague who blames the previous team, the previous government, the weather. The first half is almost never quoted by itself, because nobody needs a proverb to claim credit.

real: terrible, dreadful, hopeless — the review's harshest everyday adjective, for food, service, grades, and a team's defence
note: This module's 형편 + M1's 없다 on the 있다-chassis, fused into one adjective: the state of things does not exist. 형편 is one's means, how things stand — and when they stand nowhere, the word for it is the one every one-star review reaches for: 음식이 형편없었어요 (M1's 음식), 형편없는 점수 (M15's 점수, in the badge from M24), 형편없는 경기 (M17's 경기) for the match the defence slept through. Harsher than M29's 나쁘다, colder than M17's 별로, and one word with no space, the way 맛없다 and 재미없다 fused before it. The noun keeps its money sense in 형편이 어렵다; the adjective has forgotten money entirely.

lit: to look at (someone's) circumstances for them
real: to make allowances, cut someone slack — the request 사정 좀 봐주세요 is how you ask a landlord, a teacher, or a traffic cop to bend
note: This module's 사정 as the object of M1's 보다 through the favour machine of M9 (봐 + 주다): to look at the circumstances on someone's behalf — and looking, in Korean, is agreeing to see them. 사정 좀 봐주세요 (좀 — M9's 조금 clipped, softening it) is the sentence said at the counter after the deadline, to the landlord in a thin month, to the officer with the ticket book open; the answer 사정은 알겠는데 (I see your situation, but — -는데 from M53) is the polite refusal it usually meets. The reverse, 사정없이 (without regard to circumstances — 사정 + M1's 없다 adverbed), means mercilessly: 사정없이 때리다 (때리다 — to hit, riding frozen; it belongs to M94). Personal circumstances are the one currency Korean bureaucracy will sometimes accept; this is the phrase that offers them.

real: the 'she' Korean built for print in the early twentieth century — read on every page of every novel, said aloud by nobody
note: This module's 그녀 is younger than the grandmothers who read it: Korean had no separate 'she' until novelists of the 1920s, translating and imitating Japanese fiction, copied 彼女 (that-woman) character for character — M29's 그 + the 女 of M4's 여자 — to give their heroines a pronoun. Before that, prose used 그 for anyone, and it still does for men; 그녀 is the only gendered pronoun the language owns, and it never crossed into the mouth. Say 그녀 in conversation and you sound like a subtitle; the mouth points (그 사람, M55's 걔) or names (M4's 씨). The complaint that it is a Japanese import and should be retired surfaces every decade, and every decade the novels keep it. A word that shows what the written register is: not older Korean, but a Korean built for the page.

lit: you (casual) · you (courtly) · you (formal/spousal) · that side · Mr./Ms. So-and-so
real: the ladder of you's — five rungs, and the safe answer is the top one: a name or a title, never a pronoun
note: Korean avoids 'you' and this module completes the reasons. M19's 너 ('반말-only') is for real friends and children. 자네 is said DOWN by a senior to a grown junior — the professor, the father-in-law — on the courtly 하게 level; hear it, don't say it. M32's 당신 is the formal, spousal, careful you — dear between spouses, a fight-starter to a stranger. 그쪽 — M29's 그 + M23's 쪽, that side — is the stranger's you: the other party at a counter, a blind date's first minutes, a phone call with a wrong number. And the rung everyone actually uses is not a pronoun at all: the name with M4's 씨, or the title (선생님, 사장님 — M4, M9). The written register adds one more: 그대 (thou — riding frozen), the you of poems and song lyrics only. Rule from M32 still holds: the more formal the 'you', the more dangerous it is to say.

real: three ways to say 'person' after a number or a pointer — one counts, one counts with respect, one judges
note: M5's 명 note put it in one line: '네 명 (four people). The honorific version is 분.' — 세 명 counts the room, 세 분 counts the guests, and neither has an opinion about anyone. This module's 놈 is the third slot with the opinion built in: 세 놈 = three rascals, 그 놈 = that guy (contempt or affection, tone decides). All three are dependent — they need a number or a pointer in front — and the radar is register: 분 upward (손님 두 분), 명 level (학생 두 명), 놈 downward (나쁜 놈 둘). The drama runs on the third; the restaurant on the first two. Its female twin 년 exists, is only ever an insult, and is not for learners to deploy — file it under words to recognize in a shouting match, not to use.

real: minding what other people think — dressing, ordering, choosing a job, or parking with the neighbors' eyes in mind; the reflex Korea names in itself and half-regrets
note: This module's 의식하다 with M74's 남 ("Everyone who isn't 우리 (M4): others, strangers, other people's") as its object: to have other people switched on in your awareness. It names a whole social climate — the reason a 소개팅 outfit is chosen for the friends who will hear about it, the reason 눈치 exists at all. M42's 눈치 note called it the organ that senses what the listener knows and gave the frame "눈치를 보다 = anxiously reading the room"; 남을 의식하다 is what the organ is FOR, said from the outside. The self-help shelf's bestsellers are all built on the negative — 남을 의식하지 마세요, stop minding others — and the sentence is only sayable because the habit is universal enough to have a name. Pairs with 남의 눈 (M14's 눈) = other people's eyes, the thing being minded; 남의 눈을 의식하다 is the full form, and the shortest diagnosis of why the whole country dresses well.

lit: to be at the verge of dying
real: I'm dying — of overwork, heat, hunger, boredom, embarrassment; the everyday hyperbole for any state at its limit
note: This module's 지경 in its home frame: M14's 죽다 wears the prospective badge and 지경 names the edge — 죽을 지경이에요 = I'm at the point of dying. Nobody is: it is Korea's all-purpose 'I'm dying', filed the way English files it, and the cause slots in front on -아/어서 — 더워서 죽을 지경이에요 (M11's 덥다), 배고파서 죽을 지경이에요 (M3's 배고프다), 일이 많아서 죽을 지경이에요 (the work-일 inside M2's 일하다, M7's 많다). The casual form loses the noun and keeps the verb — 더워 죽겠어요 (the -겠- from M49, will-die) — and the two are the same complaint at two registers: 지경 is the one you can write. Never for actual danger; the sentence about the real cliff has no room for the joke.

real: it depends on the person — the answer to every generalization, and the polite refusal to make one
note: This module's 나름 after a bare noun, closed with 이다: [noun] 나름이다 = it depends on the [noun]. M1's 사람 is the noun most often in the slot — 사람 나름이에요 answers whether Koreans like spicy food, whether the job is hard, and every other question that wanted a rule. Swap the noun and the frame keeps working: 경우 나름 (M32's 경우) = case by case, 생각하기 나름 (the -기 nominalizer from M13 on M10's 생각하다) = it's how you look at it, 하기 나름 = it depends how you do it. Radar: 나름대로 (with 대로 from M54) means in one's own WAY; 나름이다 with no particle means it DEPENDS — the noun stands bare, the judgment stands relative. The sentence Korean reaches for when it declines to judge — on a shelf otherwise full of judging.

lit: even sleeves brushing is a bond
real: no meeting is an accident — the proverb Korea says about strangers, ex-lovers, and the person who sat next to you on the train
note: This module's 인연 in its most-quoted sentence. 옷깃 (the collar or lapel of M7's 옷 — riding frozen) + only-만 from M30 + 스치다 (to brush past — riding frozen) on -아/어도 from M39: even if only your collars brush, it is 인연 — the cause-tie from a previous life that put you both on that platform. Buddhist in origin, secular in use: said warmly when two people discover they met before, said wistfully after a breakup (that was 인연 too), and said by every drama's narrator over the first accidental collision of the leads. The full form ends 인연이다; the mouth stops at 인연. Its cousin is on this shelf too — 운명 is what the meeting is CALLED once it turns out to matter; 인연 is the thread that was already there. The sentence to know before someone says it to you and expects you to smile.

real: in a word, in short — the summarizer's opener, and the polite warning that a verdict is coming
note: This module's 한마디 with M6's 로 in its by-means-of job: in one word. It fronts a sentence the way M32's 결국 ends one — 한마디로 말하면 (M4's 말하다 on -(으)면 from M20) = to put it in a word; 한마디로 대박이에요 (S1's 대박) = in short, a hit; 한마디로 안 돼요 = in a word, no. The word count is a lie: what follows is always more than one word, and often a paragraph — 한마디로 promises brevity to buy the room's attention, like the English long-story-short. The 마디 inside is a joint (of bamboo, of a finger, of a bar of music — riding frozen), so a 한마디 is one segment of speech; 몇 마디 = a few words, 두 마디 = two remarks. Written as one word; said as the throat-clearing before the verdict.

lit: you strove · you exerted effort · you suffered
real: three thank-yous for effort — and only the first is safe to send UP the ladder
note: M71 wrote the rule: 수고하다 "rates effort, and rating is a superior's privilege" — 수고하셨습니다 travels sideways and down, "never up at a boss". The M16 gap deck's 수고하셨습니다 and the M26 gap deck's 고생했어요 both live in that band. This module's 애쓰다 is the one etiquette lets you aim upward: 애쓰셨습니다 (the honorific -(으)시- from M4, the -습니다 register) does not RATE the senior's effort, it acknowledges the strain of it, and so the professor, the team lead and the visiting official can hear it without the flinch that 수고하셨습니다 causes. Calibration: to the delivery driver, 수고하세요; to the colleague, 수고하셨어요; to the friend after exams, 고생했어요; to the boss who stayed late, 애쓰셨습니다 — or, safest of all, the version M71 filed for leaving a senior, 내일 뵙겠습니다, which thanks nobody and offends no one. The verb's honorific past, 애쓰셨어요, is the everyday form of the same sentence.

lit: the further you go, a great mountain
real: it only gets worse — out of the frying pan, into the fire
note: This module's -(으)ㄹ수록 on M1's 가다, fossilized: 갈수록 = the further along you go, as time goes on — the one form of the ending every column uses. 태산 is the mountain the M56 gap deck filed as "태산 (泰山 — the great mountain of Chinese legend)" and 티끌 모아 태산 (the M43 gap deck) built from dust; here the same mountain is what rises in front of you every time you round a bend. Said with a sigh when a problem solved reveals a bigger one: 갈수록 태산이네요. The proverb is the ending's whole meaning in four syllables — the more of the one, the more of the other — and its verb is the plainest verb you own.

real: you too? — the betrayal particle, Brutus in two syllables
note: 마저 on M19's 너: not 'even you' as a surprise (that would be 너조차 — even someone as unlikely as you) but 'even you' as the last one standing — everyone else has gone, and now you go too. The particle of the final straw carries the whole weight of a betrayal when the noun is a person: 너마저 떠나면 (M23's 떠나다 with -(으)면 from M20) = if even you leave… is a ballad title, a drama line, and a text message. Sort the three evens on a person: 너도 = you as well (M2's 도), 너조차 = even you, of all people (the bottom of the list), 너마저 = even you, the last (the end of the list). Only 마저 makes the listener guilty.

real: I just can't — it's not going to happen, and I've tried
note: This module's 도저히 in its native habitat: in front of 안 되다 (M10's 되다 in its it-works job, M3's 안) with the -겠- of M49 adding the speaker's verdict — 도저히 안 되겠어요 = there's no way this is going to work, I give up. It is the sentence you say putting down the wrench, the essay, the diet, the relationship; the 도저히 says you reached the bottom (到底) and found nothing there. Register-flexible: 도저히 안 되겠다 to yourself, 도저히 안 되겠어요 to the boss, 도저히 안 되겠습니다 to the client. Radar: 절대 안 돼요 with M39's 절대 forbids; 도저히 안 되겠어요 surrenders.

real: the candlelight demonstrations — Korea's signature form of peaceful mass protest: families in a square holding candles, and on three occasions, a government changed
note: This module's 시위 with 촛불 in front: M25's 초 (the candle) + M13's 불 (fire, light) with the linking-ㅅ that M82's 바닷물 note documented — 촛불, candlelight, said 초뿔. The form was born in 2002 (a vigil for two schoolgirls killed by a US army vehicle), returned in 2008 (against beef imports), and in the winter of 2016–17 filled 광화문 광장 (M23's 광장; 광화문 the gate, riding frozen) with over a million people every Saturday until the president was removed from office — the 촛불 혁명, as the papers named it (혁명 — revolution, frozen). The candle is the point: it says the crowd is peaceful, that it will be there after dark, and that it has brought its children. Where the 1987 of this module's 민주화 note is the story of 시위 that turned into tear gas, 촛불 시위 is the story the next generation tells instead — the same word, a different light. Pairs with M32's 국민 and today's 여론: a 촛불 시위 is public opinion made visible.

real: the national ID card — issued at seventeen, carried by every adult, demanded by every bank, phone shop, and bar; the number on it is your identity in every system in the country
note: Three words from three modules: this module's 주민 (the resident) + M64's 등록 (the registration — putting it on the books) + the proof-證 that M83's 학생증 decoded (its note filed 신분증 as the ID card, riding frozen — 주민등록증 is the one it meant). Every Korean is registered to an address at birth, and at seventeen the card comes with a 13-digit 주민등록번호 (M20's 번호): birthdate, then a check number, and the number follows you into every form, every contract, every online sign-up — which is why Korean websites ask for it and why leaking it is a national scandal. The 동사무소, the neighbourhood office (riding frozen), issues it; the M27 gap deck's 민증 검사 at the door of a bar is a 주민등록증 check by its nickname, 민증. Foreigners carry its twin, the 외국인등록증 (M23's 외국인 + the same 등록증) — the card the immigration office gives you, and the one this course's readers will hold first.

real: the ruling party and the opposition — the pair every political headline is written between
note: Two words built on this module's 정당, and the hanja names the seating plan. 여당 is 與黨: 與, to give or to be WITH — the party with the government, the one that holds the presidency. 야당 is 野黨: 野, the open field — the 야 of M17's 야구 ("야 (field) + 구 (ball)") — the party out in the field, outside the palace walls. The two swap places at every 대통령 선거 (M32's 대통령 + today's 선거), and the newspaper's third word, 여야 (ruling-and-opposition, riding frozen), names them as a pair: 여야 합의 = a cross-party agreement. RADAR: this 여 is 與, not M78's 여 (the female prefix) and not the 輿 of today's 여론 — three 여s, three characters, and a headline can carry all of them: 여당은 여론에 따라 (Part 3), the ruling party according to public opinion.

lit: to be driven into the mould
real: stereotyped, formulaic, stuck in a rut — said of a life, a speech, a drama plot, or a way of thinking that comes out of the same cast every time
note: This module's 틀 with 박히다 — to be driven in, to be stuck fast (riding frozen; the passive of 박다, to hammer in). A thing cast in a mould comes out the same shape every time: 틀에 박힌 생활 (M29's 생활) = a life in a rut, 틀에 박힌 표현 (M33's 표현) = a stock phrase, 틀에 박힌 사고 방식 (this module's 방식; 사고, thinking, riding frozen) = formulaic thinking. Mostly in the badge -(으)ㄴ from M24 — 틀에 박힌 — in front of a noun, and mostly as a complaint. The escape is on the same shelf: 틀을 깨다 (M36's 깨다) = to break the mould. Korean office culture is accused of the first and advertises the second, and a 신입사원 (the new-hire compound M43's 사원 note filed) learns which one the boss actually rewards.

real: for a few reasons at once; while I'm at it — the adverb that admits a trip had more than one purpose, and softens the fact that seeing you was not the only one
note: The 兼 of this module's -(으)ㄹ 겸, doubled with 事 (the affairs-사 of M43's 사업, "事業 affairs-work") into a four-syllable adverb, riding frozen as a whole. 겸사겸사 왔어요 = I came for a couple of reasons — one of which is you, and the sentence tactfully does not rank them; 겸사겸사 들렀어요 (M74's 들르다) = I dropped by while I was in the area anyway. Where -(으)ㄹ 겸 names the second purpose (운동도 할 겸), 겸사겸사 waves at all of them without naming any, which is exactly what makes it polite: the visit was not a special trip, so nobody owes anybody. Sort it from -는 김에, the other glue on this shelf: 김에 rides an occasion that already existed; 겸사겸사 admits the occasion was several things at once. Reduplication is Korean's adverb factory — 차례차례 (M46's 차례, doubled — in turn), 하나하나 (M5's 하나) — and this is its most sociable product.

lit: since the words have come out
real: now that it's come up; while we're on the subject — the phrase that turns a passing mention into the thing you actually wanted to say
note: This module's -는 김에 in its past form, with the badge -(으)ㄴ from M24 on M28's 나오다: M4's 말 — the speech — has ALREADY come out, and the speaker rides its momentum. 말이 나온 김에 하나만 더 말할게요 (M5's 하나, M9's 더, -(으)ㄹ게요 from M84) = since it's come up, let me say one more thing — the sentence in which the small talk was never small. The 김 is the steam off a pot: the topic is hot, so cook on it. Radar: the same 김 that M18's 김 note keeps apart from 김치 and the surname is a different word again from this dependent noun — four 김s, and only this one is grammar. Its cousin in the office is 온 김에 (M1's 오다) = while you're here — the phrase every visit to a colleague's desk is ambushed with.

real: don't worry about it — never mind, it's nothing, don't let it bother you
note: This module's 신경 with M10's 쓰다 in its use-job and -지 마세요 from M14 on the end: the most-said sentence on the whole shelf. Korean spends nerves the way English spends time — 신경 쓰다 = to mind, to care, to fret — so 신경 쓰지 마세요 means stop spending them on this. It is the answer to an apology (누가 커피를 쏟았을 때), the end of an argument you have decided not to have, and the polite lie every host tells. Intimate: 신경 쓰지 마 (M19's 반말); to yourself, 신경 안 써 = I don't care. Its passive twin says what the phrase is for: 신경 쓰여요 (M36's 쓰이다) = it's on my mind, it bothers me — the confession the imperative is trying to cure. Radar: 걱정하지 마세요 (M14's 걱정하다) forbids worry about a FUTURE; 신경 쓰지 마세요 releases you from a thing already on the table.

real: the reply given on autopilot — the 네, 네 with nobody home behind it; the office's word for a Monday face
note: This module's 영혼 with M1's 없다 in the badge -는 from M24, on the noun inside M10's 대답하다: the answer with no soul in it. Every office knows the voice — 네, 알겠습니다 delivered while the eyes stay on the screen — and Korean names the missing ingredient exactly: not attention, not interest, but the 영혼, the soul. The phrase has spread from the reply to everything done without one: 영혼 없는 리액션 (리액션 — reaction, the loanword, riding frozen), 영혼 없는 박수 (박수 — applause, riding frozen), 영혼 없이 일하다 = to work with the soul switched off, the condition M5's 월요일 induces. Radar with the sort in the word note: 정신 없는 (M34's 정신) means frantic, too much going on; 영혼 없는 means the opposite — nothing going on at all.

lit: would a sparrow pass the mill and not stop?
real: as if they could walk past — said of anyone who cannot go by a bar, a bakery, a shoe shop without going in
note: This module's 참새 on the bare 가, then the mill: 방앗간 (riding frozen — 방아 the grain-mill and the room-間 of M32's 인간, with the linking-ㅅ), the place grain is husked and spilled, which is to say a sparrow's idea of heaven. M50's 지나치다 (to pass by without stopping) carries the old rhetorical ending -랴 (frozen: would it ever? — the proverb's own grammar, not yours to build with), and M24's 그냥 makes the passing-by the unthinkable part. Said fondly, mostly of oneself, usually while already turning in at the door: 참새가 방앗간을 그냥 지나치겠어요? in the modern mouth, with the -겠- of M49 replacing the antique -랴. The bakery is the mill now, and M2's 빵 the grain; the sparrow has not changed.

real: to show what you can really do; to perform at your true level — the line every coach, teacher and interviewer says before the test, and every candidate says after it with 못
note: M26's 실력 was defined as ability you can DO — that note: "your Korean level, measured in what you can DO, not what you've memorized" — and today's 발휘하다 is the verb that lets it out where it can be seen. Before: 실력을 발휘하세요 / 실력을 발휘하길 바랍니다 = go show them, on every exam-hall door and every 면접 (M43) waiting room; after, more often, the negative — 실력을 제대로 발휘하지 못했어요 (M54's 제대로) = I couldn't perform at my level, the honest post-mortem, and 제 실력이 아니에요 = that wasn't the real me. Its neighbours on the encouragement shelf: 최선을 다하다 from M39 ("최선을 다하다 = give it everything") asks for effort, 긴장하지 마세요 from M34 ("긴장하지 마세요 = relax (said right before things get worse)") asks for calm, and 실력을 발휘하다 asks for the thing you already have. Athletes (M17's 선수) get it before the 경기 (M17), students before the 시험 (M10), and the -(으)ㄹ까 봐 of Part 5 is the fear underneath all three: 실력을 발휘하지 못할까 봐.

real: except for, apart from — the frame that carries today's 제외하다 far more often than the verb ever conjugates on its own
note: Object particle + 제외하고, the -고 from M10 frozen into a preposition: 저를 제외하고 다 왔어요 (M9's 다) = everyone came but me; 주말을 제외하고 (M2's 주말) = weekdays only; 세금을 제외하고 (M43's 세금) = before tax, on every invoice. Put the badge -(으)ㄴ from M24 on it and it modifies a noun instead: 저를 제외한 모든 사람 (M29's 모든) = everyone other than me. The spoken twin is 빼고 (M53's 빼다): 저 빼고 다 왔어요 — same sentence, no hanja; the memo says 제외하고, the friend says 빼고. RADAR: 밖에 from M39 says 'nothing BUT' and needs a negative (저밖에 없어요 = there's only me); 제외하고 says 'all EXCEPT' and takes a positive (저를 제외하고 다 있어요 = everyone's here except me). Same set, drawn from opposite edges.

real: an observation deck — the physical version of today's 전망: a place built for looking out, and the standard Korean date, school trip and tourist-bus stop
note: 전망 + 臺, the platform-臺 M51's 무대 read as "舞臺 dance-platform": the outlook, with a floor under it. Every Korean city has one and 서울 (M12) has the famous two: the tower on 남산 (M31) — walked up, or by 케이블카 (riding frozen) — whose 전망대 is ringed with 사랑의 자물쇠 (love-padlocks, riding frozen) that couples clip to the fence, and the deck on the tall 빌딩 (M50) by the 한강 (M22) where the 야경 (M22 — the night view) is the point. The verb is M28's 올라가다 (전망대에 올라가다 = go up to the deck) and the reward is M22's 경치 or 구경하다 (M22). The word carries the analyst's sense with it: 전망이 좋다 said on the deck means the view is good, said in the office means the outlook is — one word for both horizons, which is exactly what 展望 always meant.

real: silence is golden — the thing to say when someone should have said nothing, and the excuse of everyone who did
note: This module's 침묵 on the topic particle, then M60's 금 — the metal that note finally gave you bare ("金 the metal itself, at last"). The full proverb has a first half Korean rarely bothers with: 웅변은 은, 침묵은 금 (웅변 — eloquence, riding frozen; 은 — silver, riding frozen, and a homograph of the topic particle it sits beside) = speech is silver, silence is gold. Said after a meeting where someone talked too long, or to oneself before hitting send; the reply that inverts it, 침묵은 금이 아니에요 (M19's 아니다) = silence is NOT golden, is the whistle-blower's line, and the reason s_m95_lose_position_silence refuses to 침묵을 지키다. Radar: the 금 is 金 the metal; the 금 of 금지 on S2's signs is 禁, and a sign saying 침묵 금지 would mean silence is forbidden.

real: to move out of your parents' home — the milestone Korean adulthood is measured by, and the one most people reach at marriage
note: This module's 독립 + 하다, and the everyday sense outranks the national one: 독립했어요? does not ask whether your country is free — it asks whether you still live with your parents. In Korea the answer is often no until M25's 결혼하다: rents in M12's 서울 and a culture that reads a single person's flat as a small loneliness keep adult children at home, and 독립 is the word for the day that ends — 서른 살에 독립했어요 (M30's 서른, M5's 살) = I moved out at thirty. The economic version is 경제적 독립 (M32's 경제 through the -적 factory from M45) = paying your own way, which many achieve years before the flat. Radar: 독립운동 (the 운동 inside M8's 운동하다) is the history-textbook sense, the 1919 movement; the two never confuse each other because one comes with a date and the other with a moving van.

real: a competitive streak — the drive that turns a board game into a blood sport; praised in athletes, forgiven in children, watched carefully in colleagues
note: This module's 승부 + the 욕 of M45's 욕심 ("欲心 desire-heart") without the heart: the desire for the decision itself. 승부욕이 강하다 (M63's 강하다) = fiercely competitive — the phrase every sports profile uses and every job interview (M43's 면접) hears as a virtue; 승부욕이 없다 = doesn't care about winning, said with a sigh by coaches and with relief by spouses. The word is the whole module in one noun: 승부 is the win-or-lose a match exists to produce, and 욕 is wanting it more than the other side does.

lit: doing this, a big matter comes out
real: keep this up and there'll be trouble — the warning said to the child on the chair, the friend on the third drink, the colleague on the fifth all-nighter
note: This module's 이러다 with the -다가 of Part 3 clipped to -다, then M67's 큰일 (that note: "큰일 났어요! = we're in trouble") through M28's 나다 in its erupting job: if this goes on, trouble erupts. The whole force is in the tense — 나요, the present, not 날 거예요: the trouble is not predicted, it is already on its way, and only the listener can stop it. 그러다 큰일 나요 is the same sentence about what YOU are doing; 이러다 큰일 나겠어요 (the -겠- of M49) softens it to a forecast, which is how you say it to a boss. The full -다가 form (이러다가 큰일 나요) is equally correct and slightly slower — the clipped one is the one shouted across a playground. Says 큰닐, with the wedged-in ㄴ that word's note already flagged.

real: I nearly died — of the near-miss on the road, and of the heat, the boredom, the embarrassment, the spice; the everyday hyperbole of survival
note: Part 5's -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 on M14's 죽다: the near-death that happens to every Korean several times a week. Two registers share the sentence. The literal one is real — 차에 치여서 죽을 뻔했어요 (M50's 자동차 clipped to 차, 치이다 — to be run over, riding frozen) — and the hyperbolic one is everything else: 매워서 죽을 뻔했어요 (M3's 맵다) = the spice nearly killed me, 창피해서 죽을 뻔했어요 (M42's 창피하다) = I nearly died of embarrassment, 웃겨서 죽을 뻔했어요 (M19's 웃기다). The M87 gap deck filed its cousin, 죽을 지경이다 — that note: "Never for actual danger; the sentence about the real cliff has no room for the joke" — and the two divide the work: 지경 is a state you are IN, 뻔하다 is the moment that PASSED. Casual it clips to 죽을 뻔했어 (M19's 반말) and, on a phone, to 죽을 뻔. Nobody is ever dead; the point of 뻔 is that it did not happen.

real: to lend an ear, to listen closely — what a good counsellor does, what a minister promises, what a parent asks a teenager for
note: This module's 기울이다 on M14's 귀: to tip the ear toward the speaker — the body's picture of attention, the same lean English keeps in lend an ear and Korean makes literal. It is the essay's and the podium's phrase: 국민의 목소리에 귀를 기울이다 (M32's 국민, M19's 목소리) = listen to the voice of the people, the promise on every campaign poster; 아이의 말에 귀를 기울여 주세요 (M4's 아이, M4's 말, the favour machine of M9) = please really listen to your child, the parenting column's. Sort: M2's 듣다 hears — sound arrives; 귀를 기울이다 is the act of arranging yourself so that it does. Its twin on the same verb, 관심을 기울이다 (M24's 관심), tips the mind instead of the ear; and 노력을 기울이다 (M39's 노력) tips the whole self. One verb, three things leaned into a cause.

real: supply and demand — the economy page's first law, in Korean word order: demand first, supply second, and the price where they meet
note: Today's 수요 and 공급 joined by the written 와 from M30 — M30's 와 note called it "the written and" — and the order is fixed: Korean says demand-and-supply, English says supply-and-demand, and neither will swap. 수요와 공급의 법칙 (M39's 법 with the 칙 of M39's 규칙 — 법칙, the law, riding frozen) = the law of supply and demand, the first sentence of every 경제 (M32) textbook; 수요와 공급이 맞다 (M15's 맞다) = supply meets demand; 공급이 수요를 따라가지 못하다 (M66's 따라가다, M3's 못) = supply cannot keep up — the phrase under every housing headline. The pair is the shelf's whole thesis: two Sino nouns, one particle, and a price that M21's 가격 and today's 물가 both report on.

lit: the price level has climbed too much
real: everything's gotten so expensive — the national grumble, said at the checkout, at the market, and at the start of every conversation about money
note: Today's 물가 on the bare 가, M11's 너무, and M22's 오르다 in the past — the verb whose note listed "Mountains, stairs, and prices — all things that 오르다". The economy page writes it as 물가 상승 (상승 — a rise, riding frozen) and the mouth says this; both mean the same 라면 (M3) costs more than it did. Its answers are a shelf of their own: 월급은 안 오르는데 (M16's 월급, -는데 from M53) = but salaries don't; 장보기가 무서워요 (장을 보다 — to shop for groceries, riding frozen; M24's 무섭다) = I'm scared to go shopping; and the reckoning this module's sentence deck runs, 월급이 줄어든 셈이에요. Radar: 물가가 비싸요 (M7's 비싸다) is what a visitor says about a city; 물가가 올랐어요 is what a resident says about this year.

real: the two-tier job market — the chaebol and everyone else: the same job title, a different salary, a different pension, a different answer to 어디 다녀요?
note: M64's 대기업 — that note read it as "大 (big) + 企 (stand up to) + 業 (business)" — against today's 중소기업, the pair M90's 기업 note called "the other half of every economic headline". The sort is not size but a class line: a 대기업 (삼성, 현대 — the 재벌, riding frozen) pays more, promotes slower, and answers 어디 다녀요? (M16's 다니다) with a name everyone knows; a 중소기업 employs most of the country and answers with a shrug. The gap between the two 월급 (M16) is the number the economy page prints every spring, and 취직 (M43) at a 대기업 is the reason for the 스펙 (the résumé's specs, riding frozen) that the exam shelf of M44 was built around. Radar: 중견기업 (a mid-sized firm, riding frozen) is the tier the ministry invented so that nobody has to be in the middle.

real: the sweet, milky instant coffee of the old tearooms — coffee, creamer and sugar in equal spoonfuls, stirred in a thick cup; now a nostalgic order, a flavour of ice cream, and the ancestor of the coffee-mix stick in every office drawer
note: This module's 다방 + M1's 커피: the drink the tearoom sold for forty years, before M2's 카페 arrived with beans and a grinder. The recipe is a ratio, not a roast — 둘둘둘 (two, two, two — riding frozen: two spoons each of instant coffee, 프림 (the creamer, riding frozen) and M3's 설탕), and the 마담 who made it (riding frozen) was judged, as the sentence deck has it, on 커피 솜씨. The 믹스커피 stick (riding frozen) is the same drink pre-measured; ordering a 다방 커피 today, in a place that will make one, is ordering the decade with it. 카페 커피 is what you drink; 다방 커피 is what your parents did.

real: Teachers' Day, the fifteenth of May — carnations pinned on lapels, a song every Korean can sing, and a gift culture so fraught that many schools now simply close for the day
note: This module's 스승 with 의 and M11's 날 — the one day the relationship word, not the address word, goes on the calendar: it is never 선생님의 날. The date is King Sejong's birthday (세종대왕, riding frozen — the teacher of the nation, since the alphabet). The song is the phrase the 스승 entry filed: 스승의 은혜는 하늘 같아서 (은혜 — grace, a debt of kindness — riding frozen; M24's 같다 in -아/어서) = a teacher's grace is like the sky, sung by a classroom to a teacher trying not to cry. The 카네이션 (riding frozen) goes on the chest; the gift went into the gray zone after the anti-graft law (riding frozen, 2016) — which is why a handwritten 편지 (M27) is now the correct present, and why 스승의 날 is the day Korea argues about what it owes the people who taught it.

real: the soap that has gone all the way to the bottom — amnesia, secret births, a villain who poisons the rice, a slap per episode; watched by everyone, admitted by no one
note: 막장 (riding frozen) is the working face at the end of a mine shaft — as far down as you can go — and Korean uses it for anything that has hit rock bottom; hang M17's 드라마 on it and you have the genre the 극 entry called the -극 rail run off the end. The 막장 드라마 is the daily-morning serial and the weekend family saga at their most shameless: the 소재 is always revenge, the 비극 is always someone else's, and the ratings are enormous. Critics use the word to scold; viewers use it to recommend — 완전 막장인데 재밌어 (S1's 완전, M7's 재미있다) = it's total trash and I can't stop. The stage word (극) and the loan word (드라마) sit in the same phrase, which is this module's register pair caught in the act.

real: staff only; authorized personnel only — the sign on the door behind the counter, the stage door, the server room, the hospital ward at night
note: Four nouns and no verb, the sign register S2 taught you to read: today's 관계자 (the persons concerned), M55's 외 (that note: "외 is sign-Korean"), M52's 출입 (entry and exit as one word) and S2's 금지. M55 read the whole line for you when it taught 외 — "관계자 외 출입 금지 (staff only; 관계자 = 'persons concerned', riding frozen) guards half the doors in Korea" — and the frozen word thaws today. Its siblings hang on the same rail: 외부인 출입 금지 (today's 외부 with the person-suffix — outsiders keep out), 공사 중 출입 금지 (S2's 공사 and 중 — no entry, work in progress). Read the sign, then read yourself: if you are not a 관계자, the door is not yours.

real: exam hell — the years a Korean teenager spends inside the university-entrance machine: the 학원 nights, the November 수능, the single day that files a life
note: Today's 입시 with 지옥 (地獄 — hell, riding frozen; its heaven, 천국, rides with it): the phrase every education column has used for half a century. M15 toured the machinery — 학원 and the 수능 that M32's 교육 note called "The national obsession M15 toured" — and 입시 지옥 is the machinery's name for itself. The parts you own: 고삼 (the third-year high-schooler, said with a sigh — riding frozen) is the person inside it, M44's 합격 is the exit, 입시 부정 (today's 부정) is the scandal when someone buys the exit. On 수능 day the country reroutes its planes so the listening section is not disturbed; that fact is the whole concept in one detail.

lit: to not sort means and methods
real: to stop at nothing, by any means necessary — said of the ruthless competitor, the desperate parent, the villain in episode nine
note: Today's 수단 and M32's 방법 joined by 과 from M3, then M66's 가리다 in its sorting job — that note filed "시비를 가리다 (settle right from wrong" — under the -지 않다 long negation from M28: to not sort the means from the methods = to use any of them. The pair is the module's own lesson: 수단 is WITH WHAT, 방법 is HOW, and refusing to sort either is what ruthlessness looks like in Korean. Its cousin on the same verb is the picky eater: 음식을 가리다 = to be fussy about food, 가리는 음식이 없어요 = I eat anything. One verb sorts food and scruples alike; dropping it is a compliment at the table and an indictment in the boardroom. Says 가리지 안타 — the ㅎ of 않 aspirates the ㄷ.

real: dumbfounding, jaw-dropping — in either direction: unbelievably good (기가 막히게 맛있어요) or outrageously bad (기가 막혀서 말이 안 나와요)
note: Today's 기 (氣) with M12's 막히다 — that note: "길이 막혀요 — traffic is bad (lit. the road is blocked)" — the spirit jammed like a road. The phrase runs both ways and the tone decides: 기가 막히게 맛있어요 (-게 from M33, M1's 맛있다) = stunningly delicious, the food blogger's; 기가 막혀서 말이 안 나와요 (M4's 말, M28's 나오다, M3's 안) = I'm too stunned to speak, the customer-service call's. Fused, 기막히다 (riding frozen) is the same word with the 가 swallowed — 기막힌 맛, 기막힌 일. It sits on the shelf the word note opened: 기가 세다 (M41's 세다), 기가 죽다 (M14's 죽다), 기가 살다 (M4's 살다) — the 氣 as a person's spirit, with four verbs that press, strengthen, kill and revive it.

real: Building 101, Apt. 301 — the address every apartment dweller recites: block first, unit second; the delivery driver, the 관리실 loudspeaker and the wedding invitation all say it in this order
note: Today's 동 in its 棟 row with M84's 호 — that note: "삼백일 호 = room 301 (what the door says)" — and Sino numbers on both, M9's 백 leading. The unit number is a code: 삼백일 호 is the third floor, unit one; 천이백삼 호 is the twelfth floor, unit three — so a Korean hears the floor in the address. The blocks are numbered from 101, never from 1, which is why no 아파트 (M13) has a 일 동. The delivery question is 몇 동 몇 호예요? (M5's 몇), and the answer comes back in exactly this rhythm. Radar: the 동 in the street address above it — 역삼동, 서교동 — is the neighbourhood-洞 of M22's 동네, so a full address stacks two 동s: the 洞 you live in, then the 棟 you live in.

real: food, clothing and shelter — the three necessities, in Korean's fixed order: clothes first, roof last
note: 衣食住: the 衣 of today's 의복 + the food-食 of M1's 음식 + the live-住 M81's 주택 decoded ("住 live — a FIRST"). English puts food first; the Confucian order puts clothes first — how you are seen before what you eat — and the set is frozen: no Korean says 식의주. 의식주를 해결하다 (M56's 해결하다) = to make ends meet, the first thing a wage must do; 의식주 문제 (M7's 문제) = the problem of basic needs, the welfare page's phrase; 의식주가 해결되면 (-(으)면 from M20, the 되다 flip) = once the basics are covered. Read it by the row, the way this module reads everything: three syllables, three hanja, three words you now own the roots of.

real: a press conference — the room where the statement is read and the questions are not always answered
note: M16's 기자 in front of today's 회견: the only place 회견 lives, and the news' most-filmed room. 기자 회견을 열다 (M13's 열다) = to hold one; 긴급 기자 회견 (M84's 긴급) = an emergency press conference, called when something has gone wrong; 사과 기자 회견 (the noun of M33's 사과하다) = the apology press conference, a Korean genre of its own — a celebrity or a chairman at a podium, a bow held for a counted number of seconds, and the photographers timing it. The 성명 is what is read; the 회견 is the reading of it; what comes after is 질문 (M10's 질문), and 질문은 받지 않겠습니다 — no questions — is the line that tells you how bad it is.

real: so-called — the columnist's scare quotes, in one word
note: Today's 소위 before a noun does what English does with two raised fingers: 소위 전문가 (M58's 전문가) — the 'experts'; 소위 명문대 — the 'top' universities; 소위 선진국 (M97's 선진국) — the 'developed' world. The word claims only that the noun is what people CALL it, and the eyebrow supplies the rest. It is print-only: aloud, Koreans reach for 이른바 (riding frozen — the native twin, warmer, and just as skeptical) or for the plain 말하는, or they simply pause. Rule of thumb for a reader: a 소위 in an editorial means the writer disagrees with the noun; a 소위 in a report means the writer is quoting a label they did not choose. Either way the quotation marks are already there — do not add a second pair.

real: a losing proposition, a deal not worth making — about business, favours, marriages and studying abroad
note: Today's 손해 + M1's 보다 in the badge -는 from M24 + M43's 장사: the trade that takes a loss. Its mirror is the idiom M43's 장사 note filed — "남는 장사 = a deal that leaves something over — worth doing" — so the pair gives you both verdicts: 남는 장사 (worth it) and 손해 보는 장사 (not). 손해 보는 장사는 안 해요 = I don't do deals that lose, the shopkeeper's creed and everyone else's; 그건 손해 보는 장사야 = you're getting the worse end of that. 장사 keeps the market-stall register even when the deal is a relationship, which is why the phrase lands as a friend's warning and not an accountant's. The verb inside it is the same 보다 that runs 이익을 보다 in M43's 이익 note — in Korean you SEE both your profit and your loss, and the trade is what showed them to you.

real: are you with a group? is anyone joining you? — the host's first question at the restaurant door, the hotel desk and the tour bus, before any table is given
note: Today's 일행 on the bare 이 with M1's 있다 in the honorific -(으)세요 from M4: the sentence Korean hospitality opens with, because the seat depends on the count. The answers are Ring 1: 네, 두 명이에요 (M5's 명), 아니요, 혼자예요 (M10's 혼자), or 일행이 곧 와요 (M10's 곧) — the last one is why the deck's tour guide says 일행이 곧 도착할 테니까. The lower-register twin is 몇 분이세요? (M5's 몇 with the honorific people-counter 분 — riding frozen, a homograph of the minutes-분 M5 taught) = how many of you; 일행이 있으세요? asks not how many but whether you belong to anyone here. Hear it, and count before you answer.

real: under review; we're looking into it — the email reply that is neither yes nor no, and the status a proposal can hold for months
note: Today's 검토 hung on S2's 중, whose note called it "The busy-sign machine" (영업 중, 공사 중, 통화 중, 회의 중). The office adds its own sign: 검토 중입니다 = it is under review — the answer a 기획팀 (today's 기획 with M16's 팀) gives when the decision is someone else's, or nobody's. The verb form, 검토하고 있습니다, says the same thing with a person in it; 검토 중 removes the person, which is exactly why it is preferred. Its siblings on the desk: 진행 중 (M97's 진행) = in progress, 확인 중 (M20's 확인하다, the noun inside) = checking. Read 검토 중 in a reply and translate it as: not yet, and possibly not ever.

real: passing in first place — the top scorer on a national exam, named in the newspaper, interviewed about their study habits, and asked which 학원 they attended
note: Today's 수석 in front of M44's 합격 ("合格 fit-the-frame"): to fit the frame and to sit in the first seat while doing it. The phrase is a genre — every year the 수능 (the exam M15 toured and M32's 교육 note called "The national obsession M15 toured") and the bar exam produce a 수석 합격자 (the person-者 of M50's 운전자), and the papers print the same interview: 교과서 위주로 공부했어요, I mostly studied the textbook, which nobody believes. Its shelf-mates: 수석 졸업 (M44's 졸업) = top of the graduating class, 수석 입학 (M44's 입학) = entering first in the class. The gap the phrase closes: M30's 첫째 is first in a line; 수석 is first in a country.

real: to find one's tongue — the toddler's first flood of sentences, the shy guest who finally talks after the second glass, and the language learner's breakthrough: the day the Korean stops jamming and comes out
note: Today's 트이다 on 말문 — M4's 말 + M6's 문, the gate the words come through, riding frozen as a compound though you own both halves: the gate opens, and speech pours. 아이가 말문이 트였어요 (M4's 아이) = the child has started talking in earnest — the parents' sentence, usually said with pride and a little alarm; 한국어 말문이 트였어요 (M1's 한국어) = my Korean has come unstuck — the one you are working toward, and the one this module's last sentence concedes with -기는 하다 from M92. Its opposite is on a road you already know: 말문이 막히다 (M12's 막히다 — the 히 of the passive party of M36 on 막다) = to be stuck for words, the gate jammed shut. Same gate, two verbs: one from the passive party, one from today's shelf; the learner lives between them.

real: every nook and cranny — thoroughly, into every corner: how the cleaner cleans, how the tourist sees a city, how the auditor reads the books
note: Today's 구석 doubled, and the doubling means thoroughness — the same trick as 빨리빨리 (M12's 빨리, the M8 gap deck's national tempo): say the corner twice and you have been to all of them. 구석구석 청소했어요 (M8's 청소하다) = cleaned every corner — the pre-visit housework, the 대청소 before 설날; 서울을 구석구석 돌아봤어요 (M52's 돌아보다, in its look-around job) = saw every corner of Seoul, the travel blog's boast; 구석구석 살피다 (M93's 살피다) = to go over it in detail, the inspector's. Sort against M50's 곳곳 (everywhere, here and there — the written one): 곳곳 is scattered points on a map; 구석구석 is the inside of one space, exhausted. Says 구석꾸석 — the doubling tightens the second ㄱ.

real: slapdash, any old how — the doubled adverb for work done to be finished rather than done: the half-wiped table, the skimmed report, the homework copied at the bus stop
note: Today's 대충 doubled, and here the doubling does not intensify so much as ACCUSE: 대충 알아요 is an honest approximation; 대충대충 했어요 is a confession. The frame it lives in is the scolding — 대충대충 하지 마세요 (-지 마세요 from M14) = don't do it any old how, the boss's line, the coach's, the parent's over homework; and the shrug turned on oneself: 대충대충 살아요 (M4's 살다) = I just get by, no effort. Sort the doublings you now own: 빨리빨리 (M12's 빨리) is the national tempo and half a compliment; 구석구석 (this deck) is praise for thoroughness; 대충대충 is the opposite verdict on the same job. Its Sino twin never doubles — nobody says 대체로대체로 — which is the whole register difference between M85's 대체로 and today's word in one impossible phrase.

real: don't overdo it, take it easy — the doctor's, the parent's and the trainer's one line
note: Today's 무리 in its 無理 row (the empty-無 of M39's 무조건 + the 理 of M34's 이해) with M1's 하다 and -지 마세요 from M14: don't push past reason. It is said to the patient leaving the clinic, to the friend who has been at the office until eleven, to the parent lifting the box — and the answer is always 네, 안 무리할게요, with -(으)ㄹ게요 from M84 promising what nobody keeps. The intensifier is 너무 (M11): 너무 무리하지 마세요. Sort against M39's 아무리, which sounds like it and is 아무 + 리: 아무리 무리해도 (with -아/어도 from M39) puts both in one clause and means however much you overdo it. The register is warm, not clinical: 무리하다 is the one Sino verb every Korean grandmother uses.

real: to have one's pride wounded — the hurt Korean names before anger
note: Today's 자존심 (自尊心 self-honour-heart) with M36's 상하다 in the job that note filed second — "feelings do too: 기분이 상했어요 = my feelings soured" — the same verb that spoils the milk. 자존심 상해요 = that hurts my pride; 자존심 상하게 하지 마세요 (the -게 adverbializer from M33, M1's 하다, -지 마세요 from M14) = don't wound my pride; 자존심이 상해서 (-아/어서, the Ring 1 reason) 못 물어봤어요 = I was too proud to ask. The frame explains a great deal of Korean behaviour: the friend who will not accept the money, the colleague who will not ask for help, the drama lead who walks out of the restaurant — each is protecting a 자존심 that is 상하다-able. Its mirror is the verb on the other side: 자존심을 지키다 (M26's 지키다) = to keep one's pride, which is what the walking out was for.

lit: to the full extent of devoted care
real: with all one's heart — the word for how a meal, a gift or a letter was made
note: Today's 정성 (精誠) + -껏, the native suffix that means to the limit of (riding frozen; it also builds 마음껏 = to your heart's content, on M19's 마음, and 힘껏 = with all one's strength, on M14's 힘). 정성껏 준비했어요 (M8's 준비하다) = I prepared it with all my heart — what the host says while setting down the table; 정성껏 만든 (M3's 만들다 in the badge) = lovingly made, on the sign of every home-style restaurant that wants you to know the 반찬 (M3) is not from a factory; 정성껏 모시겠습니다 (M47's 모시다) = we will serve you with all our care, the hotel's promise. It pays the phrase M94's 들이다 note ran frozen — "정성을 들이다 (정성 — devoted care, riding frozen) = put one's heart into it" — and the adverb is what that verb looks like when the work is done. A 제사 table (M99) is set 정성껏; so is a lunchbox.

lit: there is no grave that has no excuse
real: everybody has their reasons — said with a raised eyebrow when someone explains why they couldn't, and said gently when you decide to forgive them anyway
note: M39's 핑계 ran this proverb with one word frozen — "The proverb goes 핑계 없는 무덤이 없다 — no grave lacks an excuse" — and 무덤 lands today, so every syllable is now yours: M39's 핑계, M1's 없다 twice (once in the badge -는 from M24, once closing in the plain style the M32 md taught you to read), and today's 무덤. The picture is a hillside of Korean burial mounds, each one holding a person who had a reason. Use it two ways: as a shrug at somebody else's story (다 핑계 없는 무덤이 없다니까요), or as a quiet excuse for your own. Its blunter cousin is 핑계 대지 마세요, the one that 핑계 note already filed with -지 마세요 from M14.

real: I'm doomed / it's a disaster — the groan walking out of an exam hall, opening the oven, or seeing the haircut in daylight
note: Today's 망하다 in the plain past, said to nobody in particular. The literal job is a business: 가게가 망했어요 (M1's 가게) = the shop went under — 亡 doing what M66's 도망가다 decoded it to do, vanish. But the country says it hourly about things that cost nothing: 시험 망했어 (M10's 시험), 발표 망했어 (M16's 발표하다, its noun) — the same downgrade M14's 죽다 note logged when it wrote that "casual Korean 'dies' of hunger, heat, and homework hourly". Register: 망했다/망했어 is casual and self-directed; you do not say it about someone else's work to their face. Its polite ceiling is 잘 안됐어요, and the fuller groan adds S1's 완전 in front: 완전 망했어.

real: my mouth is watering — said at a photo of 삼겹살, at the smell from a 시장 stall, or by a caption on every food show in the country
note: Today's 침 with 고이다 (to pool, gather — riding frozen), the verb M82's 빗물 note already ran once: "빗물이 고이다 (고이다 — to pool, riding frozen)". Rain pools in a dip in the road; saliva pools in the mouth — one verb for anything that collects where it cannot drain. Said as 침이 고여요, or, of a picture, 보기만 해도 침이 고여요 (only-만 from M30, -아/어도 from M39) = just looking at it makes my mouth water. Its neighbour on the same shelf is 군침이 돌다 (군침 — watering-at-the-mouth saliva, riding frozen; M37's 돌다) — the food writer's version, where 침이 고이다 is the plain one. And keep the radar from the entry: this 침 is the spit, not M2's 아침, not the sleep-침 of M6's 침대.

real: well, true enough — a whole concession in two syllables: you grant the other person's point, out loud, before going on with your own
note: 하기는 (frozen) worn down until the -기는 하다 from M92 could stand alone as a turn. Someone explains why they were late and you say 하긴; someone says the price was unreasonable and you say 하긴, 비싸긴 했어요 (M7's 비싸다) — granted, it WAS expensive.
