It has two tones and both are common: nodding (하긴 그래요, M29's 그렇다 — fair enough, you're right) and half-retracting your own last sentence (하긴, 제가 잘못 봤어요, M15's 맞다 kin). Sort it from the neighbours: M85's 다만 qualifies what YOU are about to say, M39's 그래도 pushes back after conceding, and 하긴 simply hands the point over. Korean conversation rewards the speaker who concedes first, and this is the cheapest way to do it.

real: the evening study session Korean high-schoolers sit through after class — officially voluntary, historically compulsory, universally clipped to 야자
note: Today's 자율 (self-rule) plus M44's 학습 and 야간 (night-time — riding frozen), and the joke is in the middle word: the 자율 that names it is the one thing it never was. School ends, dinner is eaten in the cafeteria, and the same students return to the same desks until ten or eleven at night; 야자 하다 = to do the evening session, 야자 빼다 (M53's 빼다) = to get out of it. The word has softened since — many schools now really do let students choose — but 야자 survives as the name of an era, the way M15's 학원 names an industry. Say the full phrase to a Korean adult and they will shorten it back to two syllables before answering.

real: ASAP — the closing line of Korean work email, and a demand disguised as a measurement
note: Today's 최대한 on M12's 빨리, the pairing M63's 최대 had already filed as "the deadline's national adverb". It is politer than an actual deadline and far less kind: a date can be negotiated, 최대한 빨리 cannot, because it only asks for your maximum. 최대한 빨리 보내 주세요 (M16's 보내다, -아/어 주세요 from M9) = send it as soon as you possibly can; 최대한 빨리 처리하겠습니다 (M91's 처리, -겠- from M49) is the answer it demands. It sits one generation along from 빨리빨리, which the M8 gap deck filed as the national tempo — the same instinct, wearing a Sino suit and a business-email signature.

real: your university entry year, worn as a rank for life — the number two Korean students trade before their names, and the one that decides who speaks politely to whom, even when the junior is the older person
note: Today's 학번 with the fact underneath it: a Korean campus sorts people by the year they came IN, not the year they were born. 십칠 학번 = the class of 2017, in Sino numbers always; 학번이 어떻게 되세요? establishes rank without asking M4's 나이. M58's 선배 note already wrote the law — "age is irrelevant, ENTRY DATE is everything" — and the 학번 is that law made countable: one 학번 ahead makes you a 선배, and a 후배 two years older still hands over M19's 존댓말, in the M69's 동아리 and in the office they both join later, because the 학번 travels off campus with them. It also quietly explains the people who are a year out of step with their age-mates, and nobody has to say why. English has a graduating class; Korean has an entering class, and it is also a rank.

real: in the first place, to begin with — the adverb that rewinds past the whole argument and rules that the thing should never have started
note: Today's 애초 with M1's 에, and it is almost the only shape the word takes. It is a retroactive verdict, not a time word: the speaker steps back behind the current row and cancels its premise. 애초에 계획이 잘못됐어요 (M8's 계획, M63's 잘못되다) = the plan was wrong from the start; 애초에 무리였어요 (M103's 무리) = it was never going to work — the sentence a Korean post-mortem opens with; 애초부터 (M6's 부터) hardens it further. Sort it against the two neighbours you own: M57's 원래 reports how a thing has always been ("원래 그래요 = that's just how it is: the national shrug"), and M46's 최초 is history's first ("처음 is YOUR first time; 최초 is history's"). 애초 is neither — it is this affair's starting line, revisited in order to blame it. Use it and you are no longer discussing the problem; you are discussing whether there should have been one.

lit: (from 마노라, an old court title for a person of rank)
real: my old lady — a husband's blunt, affectionate word for his own wife: warm between spouses and among men of a certain age, and a small insult in any other mouth
note: Today's 마누라, and the reason it needs a whole card: Korean has four words for wife and they are sorted by WHO IS SPEAKING and WHOSE WIFE IT IS, not by politeness alone. M27's 아내 is the neutral one you write on a form ("Your own wife. Someone ELSE's wife gets the honorific 부인"); M27's 부인 is the other man's; M58's 사모님 is your boss's or your teacher's; 와이프 (frozen, the Konglish) is what husbands under fifty say; and 마누라 is the bottom rung, a husband's own, said with the fondness of long use — 우리 마누라 (M4's 우리). The drift is the joke: 마누라 was 마노라, a court title for a person of rank, and fell the whole way down, the same slide M27's 아줌마 took from 아주머니. The three rules a learner must keep: never about another man's wife, never upward, and never by a woman about herself. Keep it in the recognition drawer — you will hear it in every drama about a marriage over twenty years old, and you will never need to say it.

lit: to do the pretending of not-knowing
real: to play dumb — to look straight at a thing and act as if you had not seen it, whether out of kindness, cowardice, or self-preservation
note: M4's 모르다 under the badge -는 from M24 with today's 척하다 behind it, and the pieces are all ordinary — it is the social weight that makes it a gap entry. Korean rates this manoeuvre, and the rating depends on M42's 눈치: pretending not to notice a colleague's mistake in front of the boss is tact, and pretending not to notice the bill arriving is not. Its twin 못 본 척하다 (M3's 못, M1's 보다) narrows it to the eyes = to look the other way, and 알면서 모르는 척하다 (M4's 알다, -(으)면서 from M38) is the accusation: you KNEW. The casual form is the one you will actually hear — 모르는 척하지 마 (-지 마세요 from M14, dropped to the intimate style) — and a Korean who says 그냥 모르는 척했어요 is usually telling you they chose peace over being right.

real: that's not fair — I didn't do it, or I did it and I had a reason, and nobody is listening
note: Today's 억울하다 in the plain polite form, and it is one of the hardest words in this course to translate because English splits it: unfair is a verdict on the situation, 억울하다 is what the wronged person FEELS, out loud, in the first person. The child sent out of the classroom says 억울해요; so does the drama's defendant, and so does the employee whose idea got someone else the credit. Grammar to go with it: 억울하면 출세해라 (출세 — getting on in the world, riding frozen; -(으)면 from M20) is the country's bleakest piece of advice — if you feel wronged, go get powerful — and 억울한 일을 당했어요 (M86's 당하다, whose note calls it Korean's "get-[noun]-ed") is the calm report of the same thing. Register warning: it is not a complaint about the weather or a queue — reach for it only when a person has judged you wrongly, or it will land as melodrama.

real: to blow the lot — to lose money all at once through a bad investment, a scam, or one spectacular decision
note: M9's 돈 with today's 날리다, which is M28's 날다 pushed through the causative party of M37: you did not drop the money, you launched it. The picture is a banknote going out of the window, and Korean keeps it for losses that were sudden and at least partly your own doing — 주식으로 돈을 날렸어요 (M97's 주식) is the commonest frame of all. Sort the three: 돈을 쓰다 (M10's 쓰다) spends it on purpose, 돈을 잃다 (M28's 잃다) loses it the way you lose a wallet, and 돈을 날리다 loses it with a decision attached. Its cousin runs without the money: M49's 날아가다 is what the unsaved file does, in the M79 sentence 저장 안 한 파일이 다 날아가 버렸어요 — one verb family for everything that leaves in a hurry and does not come back.

real: to get an earful, to take flak — what you do when a decision goes public and the internet, the neighbours, or your mother get hold of it
note: Today's 욕 with M1's 먹다, and the whole idiom is in the verb: Korean does not receive criticism, it swallows it. 욕하다 is what the other person does — the verb M31's 뉴욕 already taught you in a joke, "욕 alone is the word for a swear word (욕하다 = to curse)" — and 욕을 먹다 is the receiving end, which is why the two halves take different verbs. 사장님한테 욕 먹었어요 = the boss chewed me out; 괜히 욕먹지 마세요 (-지 마세요 from M14) = don't go inviting an earful. It belongs to the food-idiom shelf the language keeps well stocked: you eat 나이 on New Year's, you eat 미역국 and fail the exam, and you eat 욕 whenever you deserve it. The polite ceiling is 비판을 받다 (M75's 비판하다, M9's 받다) — and as that note said, "비판 (argued) is not 욕 (abuse — riding frozen, glossed)": one comes with reasons, the other comes with volume.

real: uncannily, as if by magic — said in admiration when somebody knows, finds, or predicts a thing they had no way of knowing
note: Today's 귀신 with 같이 from M9, and the ghost has almost entirely drained out of it: nothing supernatural is being claimed, only something unaccountably accurate. 엄마는 귀신같이 알아요 (M4's 알다) = Mum just KNOWS — the standard use, said by every teenager who hid something badly; 귀신같이 찾아냈어요 (M6's 찾다) = found it as if by magic; and the sports desk loves it for a striker who 귀신같이 나타나다 (M32's 나타나다) in front of goal. Register: it is a compliment, and an entirely ordinary one — you can say it to your boss. The literal ghost still exists next door in 귀신 이야기 (M24's 이야기) and 귀신이 나오다 (M28's 나오다); this idiom just borrowed the ghost's aim.

real: one round — of a game, a match, a fight, or a drinking session; the unit Korean counts contests in
note: Today's 판 in its dependent-noun row, taking the counter-contraction 한 from M5 the way the M99 md's table said every dependent noun does. 한 판 더 = one more round — the sentence that keeps a 게임 (M8) going past midnight; 마지막 판 (M15's 마지막) is the decider; 한 판 붙자 = let's have it out (M35's 붙다, the two sides sticking to each other) — a challenge, half joking and half not. The board is real and visible in the origin: 바둑 (the board game — riding frozen) 한 판, one game on one board — which is the same 板 sitting in M15's 칠판 ("칠 (paint) + 판 (board) — a painted board.") and M23's 간판. Watch the spacing, because it is the only thing separating the two senses: 한 판 with a space is one round, and 한판 closed up is the judo throw that ends the match outright.

real: can't be bothered — the whole feeling of not wanting to get up, go out, cook, reply, or change out of the clothes you are already in, said as a complete sentence and accepted as a complete reason
note: Today's 귀찮다 in the plain polite form, and it earns a gap entry because English has no single word for it: 'bothersome' describes a task, 귀찮아요 describes a person who has looked at the task and declined. It is socially legal in a way that 'I don't want to' is not — 귀찮아서 안 갔어요 (-아/어서 from M10) closes the subject among friends, and 나가기 귀찮아요 (the -기 nominalizer from M13) is a complete refusal of an evening. It points outward too, at the person causing the trouble: 귀찮게 하지 마세요 (-게 from M33, -지 마세요 from M14) = stop pestering me, and 귀찮게 해서 죄송해요 is the apology for asking a favour. The register is casual all the way down — to a boss you reach for M4's 바쁘다, or the 부담스럽다 M86's 부담 named, instead — and the country's own joke about it is 귀차니즘, 귀찮 wearing an English -ism, the ideology of not bothering.

real: how dare you — the opening of an outburst about rank, said when somebody has spoken or acted above their station
note: Today's 감히 with M10's 어떻게, and the pair is almost never finished: 감히 어떻게… trails off because the listener is supposed to supply the rest. The full shapes are 네가 감히 (M19's 너 in its subject form) = YOU dare, and 감히 어떻게 그런 말을 (M24's 그런, M4's 말) = how dare you say a thing like that. What makes it a gap entry is that the outrage is about position rather than about the act — 감히 says the speaker outranks the person they are shouting at, which is why it belongs to parents, bosses and historical dramas, and why a peer using it sounds absurd. Turned humble it flips completely: 감히 말씀드리자면 (M9's 드리다) = if I may be so bold, where the speaker is the one presuming. Modern use is mostly quotation and comedy; the sincere version still exists, and if you hear it aimed at you, the conversation is over.

lit: to have one's heart taken away
real: to be captivated, to fall for something completely — a face, a city, a song, or a person, with the speaker cast as the one it happened to
note: Today's 빼앗다 through the passive party of M36 (빼앗기다, riding frozen), and the grammar is the whole point: Korean prefers to report falling in love as a theft you were the victim of. The active exists — 마음을 빼앗다 = to steal a heart — but the passive is what people actually say about themselves: 그 사람에게 마음을 빼앗겼어요 = I lost my heart to them, 풍경에 마음을 빼앗겼어요 (M49's 풍경) = the view took me completely. Sort it against the near neighbours M19's 마음 has collected: the 마음에 들어요 M19's 마음 note explained ("'it enters my 마음' — is how things get liked") is approval, 마음을 훔치다 (M102's 훔치다) is the drama poster's version and casts the other person as the thief on purpose, and 마음을 빼앗기다 keeps the same event but moves the camera onto you. The particle is 에 for things and 에게/한테 for people, and the tense is nearly always past — it is a report, not a plan.

real: to be up against the clock — not busy for an hour but hounded for a week, with the deadline behind you and gaining
note: The M36 md printed this phrase before it printed the verb, glossing the pair in one parenthesis — "쫓기다 (be chased — 시간에 쫓기다, chased by time)" — and today both halves are yours. The picture is the whole idiom: M1's 시간 is not a container you are inside, it is a pursuer at your back, so the particle is 에, the thing-chaser particle from the M36 rule, and never 에게. Sort it against M4's 바쁘다: 바빠요 reports a full diary and can be said cheerfully, 시간에 쫓겨요 reports being beaten by it and never can. The office runs a whole family off the same verb — 일에 쫓기다, 마감에 쫓기다 (마감 — a deadline, riding frozen) — and the standard self-diagnosis, 요즘 시간에 쫓겨서 살아요 (-아/어서 from M10, M4's 살다), is what a Korean colleague says instead of admitting to being overwhelmed.

real: a slipped disc — and in Korean the word names the INJURY, not the piece of cartilage, so you do not have a disc problem, you have a 디스크
note: M14's 허리 already filed the national ailment — "허리가 아파요 — half of Korea, daily." — and this is what the clinic calls the serious end of it. The English word names an anatomical part that everyone has; the Korean loan names a condition only some people have, which is why 디스크가 있어요 = I have back trouble and 디스크에 걸리다 (M12's 걸리다, the catch-an-illness verb) = to get a slipped disc both work with no further words. Its neighbour up the spine is 목 디스크 (M14's 목). This is Rule 4 of the Konglish interlude working exactly as advertised — 'When a loanword surprises you, assume specialization, not error' — and the specialization went in a direction no English speaker would guess: not a narrower object but a different part of speech's worth of meaning.

real: the set menu served in courses — what a Korean restaurant means by 'course': dishes brought out in a fixed order at a fixed price, from the wedding hall's banquet to the pork place's set
note: Today's 코스 with the 요리 inside M3's 요리하다, and the compound is the commonest place an ordinary Korean meets the loan. The point of the phrase is the ORDER, not the food: a 코스 arrives in sequence and ends when the kitchen says so, while ordering off M3's 메뉴 dish by dish is the everyday alternative. Its Korean-register twin is the 정식 M81 taught in its second row, the set meal — 한정식 (frozen) is the Korean version of exactly this idea, one tray at a time — so the language runs the same concept through a Sino word and a loan and keeps them apart by cuisine: 한정식 for Korean, 코스 요리 for the French, Italian or Chinese restaurant. Where it really lives: 결혼식 (M25) food, and the 점심 코스 (M3's 점심) that is how an expensive restaurant sells itself at noon.

real: to be plain-looking — the old, unkind comparison Korean keeps for a face, and the reason a learner should recognize it without ever using it
note: Today's 호박 with M24's 같다, and the picture is the round orange 늙은 호박 (M35's 늙다), not the slim 애호박 the kitchen actually buys. The idiom is a museum piece with a long shelf life: 호박에 줄 긋는다고 수박 되냐 — drawing stripes on a pumpkin does not make it a watermelon (M30's 수박) — is the proverb version, and it is aimed at makeup, which is why it sits on the same page as today's 화장. Two rules for it. First, the flattering cousin is a different vegetable entirely: 호박이 넝쿨째 굴러 들어왔다 (넝쿨 — a vine, riding frozen) = a pumpkin rolled in, vine and all = unexpected good fortune, and that one you may say out loud. Second, this one you may not — Korean has moved on from it the way English moved on from its own, and the only honest use is recognizing it in a drama set in somebody's grandmother's village.

real: the household goods — the pots, the bedding, the rice cooker; and, in the other direction, how a family is getting by
note: Today's 살림 with 살이 behind it, which is M4's 살다 frozen a second time, so the word says living twice over. It faces both ways at once. Concretely it is the STUFF: 살림살이를 장만하다 (장만 — getting a household together, riding frozen) is what M78's 신혼부부 do before the wedding, and a van full of it on moving day is 이삿짐 (frozen — M54's 이사 in front of M13's 짐). Abstractly it is the STATE of a household: 살림살이가 나아졌어요 (M14's 낫다 in its get-better job) = things are easier at home now — the sentence a politician says at election time and the one a parent says quietly at the end of a hard year. The reason it earns a card is that neither English word covers both, and Korean never feels a gap: the pots and the getting-by are the same noun, because in a Korean household they have always been the same question.

real: May Day, the one public holiday most Koreans have to check their own contract about — banks and big firms close, small offices often do not, and schools stay open
note: Today's 근로 inside M64's 근로자, with 의 and M11's 날. The card is about the name, not the date. M58's 노동자 filed the other one — "May 1 is 노동절 (Labor Day — frozen)" — and both names are live: 노동절 is what the unions and the historians call it, 근로자의 날 is what the statute calls it, because the statute that created the holiday used the ministry's word. M97's 노동 drew the line this module pays off — "근로 is the ministry's word, 노동 the union's" — so the holiday is the one place in Korean where you can hear which vocabulary a speaker keeps. The other peculiarity is legal rather than lexical: it is not a 공휴일 (a red-letter public holiday — riding frozen) but a paid day off under the labour statute, which is why your Korean friend at a bank has the day and your Korean friend at a small 회사 (M2) does not.
